Evaluation of Schemes for Alleviation of Urban Poverty 
2059. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of various schemes under implementation for alleviating 
urban poverty; 
(b) how far these schemes have helped in alleviating urban poverty; 
(c> the steps taken to ensure proper implementation of   these 
schemes; 
(d) whether any evaluation/study has been conducted to determine 
effectiveness of these schemes; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O RAJAGOPAL): 
(a)The Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation has been 
implementing through the State Governments/UTs, a Centrally Sponsored Urban 
Poverty Alleviation Programme named Swarna Jayanti Shahari RozgarYojana 
(SJSRY) on all India basis, with effect from 1.12.1997 with a view to providing 
gainful employment to the urban unemployed or underemployed poc: through (i) 
encouraging the setting up of self-employment ventures by those who have read 
upto 9th standard and (ii) provision of 
418 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
wage employment by utilising their labour for construction of socially and 
economically useful public assets. The scheme is funded in the ratio of 75:25 
between the Centre and the State. 
(b) Based on the reports received from the State Governments/UTs till 
30th June, 2002 urban poor numbering about 4.40 lakh have been assisted 
through setting up of micro enterprises, 4.11 lakh received training and 402.85 
lakh mandays of work have also been generated with the utilisation of funds 
amounting to Rs. 917.27 crore (approximately). 
(c)The States/UTs are persuaded from time to time for more effective 
implementation of the scheme. In addition, close monitoring is done at the 
Central level through periodical review meetings/field visits and Quarterly 
Progress Reports. 
(d) Yes, Sir. Concurrent evaluation/study of SJSRY in six States, viz., 
Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Rajasthan and 
Uttar Pradesh have been made. 
(e) The gist of findings/recommendations of these concurrent 
evaluation/studies are given in the Statement. 
Statement 
Gist of findings/recommendations of SJSRY Schemes in six States 
ANDHRA PRADESH 
Progress of SJSRY in Andhra Pradesh: The State Government accorded 
high priority to (i) UWEP and (ii) promotion of Thrift and Credit Societies. The 
reasons for emphasis on these programmes are not difficult to guess and the 
interested parties are municipality and the CDS. It is also reported that a good 
portion of allocations under USEP was diverted towards financing of the State 
scheme "Chief Minister's Employment of Youth".The banks sanctioned loans 
at lower amounts.There is not much of link up between micro enterprises and 
training programmes. No post training evaluations about the impact of earning 
capacities of the trainees has been done. Material labour ratio of 60:40 is not 
stricity observed. 
Urban local bodies: Identification of clients on the basis of house to house 
surveys, extension work among the prospective beneficiaries and formulation of 
Locality Funds Development Plans for ensuring convergance 
419 

 
RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
of Public services in the localities of urban poor are specialized jobs and call for 
considerable investments of time and money. However, the guidelines seem to 
assume that these functions could be performed by ULB by engaging low paid 
personnel on contract basis. And also that these can be carried out with a very 
low budget. The ULBs should be endowed with authority to secure the 
needed consulting services. The staff exclusively meant for implementation of 
the programme should also receive formal training. According to the report the 
initiatives taken by the municipal authorities in promoting DWCUA groups are 
commendable.They have shown imagination in deregulating some of the 
municipal functions sand assigning them on contract basis to the DWCUA 
groups. They did not hesitate in extending guarantee on behalf of these groups and 
arranging bank loans for them. 
Community organisations: The performance of community 
organisations in the context of construction of civil works under UWEP and 
infrastructure facilities under USEP and also supervising the execution of low cost 
sanitation programme in their localities has been assessed as satisfactory. 
Commercial banks: The banks sanction smaller amount than the 
required for starting micro enterprises. For sanctioning higher amounts, they 
prefer the assurance with regard to repayment particularly from municipal 
authorities. The hesitation in extending loans is mainly on account of banks 
apprehensions about repayment.The study suggested alternative institutional 
arrangement as a solution to the persisting problem. 
Indentification of clients: It needs be clearly stated that the basis for 
determining the eligibility is the income of the household whatever may be its 
source and not limited under the wage earnings of the head of the household. 
The reliance on present scale of non-economic parameters needs review for 
proper identification of poorest among the poor. Also while the client is 
considered for subsidy provision under USER other Members of his/her family 
were found to be availing other benefits of the Yojana as well. 
Budgeting: Accumulation of unspent balances with the field agencies is 
manifestation of general systems failure. Efforts are required for adoption of 
bottom-up approach before fina'-sation of budgets. While not allowing re-
appropriation from one component to another acts as deterrent against 
420 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
funds diversion, this action could stifle local initiatives and innovations to meet 
local needs. There has also to be some incentive systems for good performance. 
Sub-critical allocations also need be avoided. Releasing funds towards the end 
of financial year is surely not the best way towards efficient financial 
management at the ULB level. The apportionment of expenditure between 
Centre and the State should be in the prescribed ratio of 75:25 in order to 
discourage the States to first book the expenditure incurred to the Central share 
and balance only to their share. This would put pressure on the State to release 
their share in time. 
Supervision and control: State should be asked to keep data in two parts 
Lethe cumulative position upto the reference year/quarter and the progress 
made during the reference period instead of its providing year-wise information 
right from inception of the scheme. Data should also be collected for other vital 
items like A&OE, investments made for strengthen of UPE Cells, expenditure on 
preparation of locality development plans, wage bill of UWEP, amount spent 
by way of stipends, tool kits, etc. and comparative data of targets and 
achievements and also much more of other requisites under the scheme. 
Review and revamping of procedures: There are duplications, wastages 
in the procedures followed in benefits provision e.g. processing of loan 
applications at different levels till receipt/process in bank. This results in 
avoidable delays and additional expenditure.The report suggests joint inspections 
by bank and ULB staff on loan applicants proposals or banks to sanction loans 
relying solely on verifications and guarantee of CDS (a big question mark). 
Local employment potential surveys must be carried out by professional 
consultants before launching training programmes. Prospective employers 
from the organised sector should be involved in the decision-making. 
Performance indicators: with the lower range of loans sanctioned under 
USEP/DWCUA, there has been lower range of subsidy too. Even the 
expenditure per trainee has been much low as compared to the ceiling fixed.The 
ceilings under UWEP are also not followed strictly, thus leading to more 
expenditure for ensuring employment. Under Community Structure while useful 
indicators could be expenditure per client on activities involved in ensuring 
convergence of services, data in that regard was not maintained. The report suggests 
that impact studies should be carried out at periodical intervals.The overall impact 
under different components of the scheme is 
421 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
reported to be satisfactory.The enterprises assisted under USEP/DWCUA are 
operating profitably/satisfactorily and because of the improved economic status, the 
women have a better say in the family decisions. 
Guidelines document Guidelines require modification. 
Perspective PlanrTargets have not been set under the Programme. 
Overall assessment Towards accomplishing objectives under the 
programme, considerable efforts have to be made towards information 
dissemination and education among the target clients. The scheme has not 
succeeded much in enlisting cooperation from NGOs.The field surveys have 
however brought out one welcome feature very clearly. This scheme has 
succeeded in good measure in promoting a new awareness among urban poor 
women. Their economic position has steadily improved and with this, they have 
a say in household decisions. They, as a group, have come to be recognized as a 
formidable force to reckon within municipal politics. 
KARNATAKA 
Indentification of BPL families 
Neither the non-economic parameters as suggested under the guidelines 
for identification of genunie beneficiaries have been applied in determining 
urban BPL families in the State of Kamataka nor they have been given 
appropriate weightage at the stage of selection of beneficiaries for extending 
benefits under SJSRY. 
Criteria for allocation of funds under SJSRY 
Instead of taking BPL population, the State of Kamataka has taken the 
total population of a local body as a base, which has induced disparities in 
allocation of funds as the percentage of BPL population varies from one ULB 
to another ULB. 
Community organisations and project administration 
The elected members of the municipalities have a vested interest in the 
selection/election of RCVs, NHC conveners and CDS office bearers and also 
they alongwith the area MLA and MPs try to interfere with the functioning of 
community-based structures 
422 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Inadequacies in the budgeting arrangements 
The budgetary arrangements should be reviewed to avoid idling of huge 
sums of money, which could have been diverted to more purposeful uses. 
Component-wise budget allocation 
Component-wise budget allocation made by DMA is not in the 
conformity with the pattern laid by this Ministry.The DMA may be advised to 
re-determine component-wise allocation. 
Self-employment through setting up micro enterprises 
2.2% of the BPL families have been financed for setting up micro 
enterprises over a period of 3 years. It has been suggested that (a) ULBs may be 
urged to develop a compendium of viable projects/activities (b) the GOI's 
instruction for creation of a district level data base may be implemented 
forthwith (c) the POs and COs should play a more active role in coordination 
with the banks. 
DWCUA 
Though the amount of subsidy should not exceed the amount of loan, 
here the subsidy has been released far in excess of the loan amount. (Loan-Rs. 
153.24 lakhs; Subsidy-Rs. 285.51 lakhs). The percentage of families benefited 
under this scheme is only 0.38 and therefore the achievement is insignificant. 
Thrift and credit society 
The number ofTCGs formed is too small considering that the number of 
BPL families is around 9 lakhs. 
Training and Infrastructure 
As per the guidelines, the ULBs are to provide infrastructure support to 
potential BPL entrepreneurs in terms of selling places in the form of Kiosks 
and rehri markets. However, this has not been done. 
Urban Wage Employment Programme (UWEP) 
The main-days of work generated has been indicated as Rs. 27.47 lakhs 
which seems to be incorrect as the expenditure on the material 
423 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
component has been reckoned as nil.  The MIS format is defective. The 
procedures followed and the records maintained are deficient. Beneficiary-wiie 
data is not available. 
Suggestions are that the procedure for employment of labour under the 
wage employment scheme may be streamlined so that the scheme benefits the 
genuine BPL households on an equitable basis. Chief executives of ULBs 
may be authorized to allow higher rates of wage. Expenditure under the scheme 
should be displayed distinctly for the material and the labour components. Non 
BPL should be offered employment only when BPL persons are not 
available. 
Administration and Office Expense 
The A&OE should be linked to total annual expenditure under SJSRY instead 
of total budgetary allocation. The MIS format is inadequate and needs to be 
modified suitably. 
Information, Education and Communication 
Though the guidelines says that the States may utilise upto 2% of their 
allocation for activities under the IEC components, the DMA founds to have not 
earmarked any funds directly under this head.The MIS format also does not 
capture any information on IEC, which needs to be modified. 
Monitoring System 
The formats of monthly progress report submitted by ULBs to DMA and 
that of the quarterly progress report submitted by DMA to the Ministry have 
inadequacies and may be reviewed and re-structured suitably. 
Impact Evaluation 
Design and conduct of the survey was faulty with the result that the poorest 
of the poor have not been identified.The way the wage employment component is 
being administered; there is no certainty that its beneficiaries are primarily BPL 
persons. The scheme has so far made hardly any impact on raising income of the 
families. However, formation of community organization with women in the 
forefront has generated general awareness among women and brought them 
together on a common platform. It is considered that the scheme if 
implemented properly has the potential of making a dent on urban poverty and 
raising the status of women and children.

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
MADHYA PRADESH 
Allocation of funds: 
The State Government has taken the total urban population of a district 
as a base instead of considering the BPL population for the purpose of allocation of 
funds. It may lead to inter-town disparities, as the town with lower percentage 
of BPL population will cet higher per capita budgetary allocation. 
Community organizations and Project Administration: 
The elected members of municipalities interfere with plans of DUDA and 
ULBs to get approval of projects outside the action plans of CDS. 
Considering the nature of duties and responsibilities of their COs, the salary 
structure and the terms and conditions of their appointment call for a review. 
Component-wise budget allocation: 
Component-wise budget allocation received by Directorate of 
Municipal Administration and Development does not conform to the pattern laid 
down by the Department of UEPA. 
Micro enterprises: 
In order to bring down the rate of rejection of loan applications and for 
timely processing the applications, DUDA may be urged to develop a 
compendium of viable projects/activities and make it available to the 
potential beneficiaries for guidance. 
DWCUA (Sellf-employment Ventures): 
The achievement under this Component te insignificant considering the 
fact that out of the total number of BPL families (11 Lakhs) the percentage 
of families benefited is only 0.06. 
Thrift and Credit Groups: 
Number of T&C groups formed is very small considering that the 
number of BPL families. Since most of theTC groups have not completed one 
year after their formation have not yet became entitled to the grant of revolving 
fund. 
Infrastructure support 
The prescribed MIS format did not seek particulars of the infrastructure 
facilities created for the urban poor. ULBs/DUDA may be urged to act as per the 
guidelines. 
425 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
Urban Wage Employment Programme: 
The Muster Rolls do not show whether or not the person employed belong 
to a BPL  family. It is suggested that the procedure for employment of labour 
under this scheme may be streamlined so that it benefits the genuine BPL 
households on an equitable basis. Expenditure under the scheme should be 
displayed distinctively for the material and the labour components. There should 
be no discrepancy between the reported man-days and actual man-days of work 
generated. Also the Muster Rolls should clearly indicate whether or not the person 
employed belongs to BPL family. 
Administration and Office Expenses: 
There is an infirmity in the guidelines in as much as they link 'A&OE' to the 
allocated funds and not to the actual expenditure. More appropriately, the 'A&OE' 
should be linked to total annual expenditure under SJSRY instead of total 
budgetary allocation. Also the MIS format is inadequate in as much as it does not 
capture information under "A&OE". Thus the MIS format needs to be modified 
suitably. 
Information, Education and Communication: 
DMAD has not earmarked any funds directly under this head although 
the guidelines provide 2% of their allocation. The monthly progress report submitted 
by DUDAs to the DMAD and the MIS format of the Ministry do not provide any 
information on 'IEC*. There is a need to rectify these deficiencies. 
Monitoring System, The formats of monthly progress report submitted by 
ULBs to DMAD and that of the quarterly progress report submitted by DMAD 
to the Ministry have inadequacies and may be reviewed and restructured 
suitably. 
Role ofNGOs: NGOs involvement could be significantly increased if they 
are involved in the process of information of groups under DWCUA and Thrift 
and Credit Societies.They could be used as pressure groups to bring about social 
pressure on defaulting borrowers. 
WESTBENGAL 
The Study Team of IIPA has observed that training given in various trades 
to women below poverty line have resulted in remarkable change of attitude, 
behaviour and tremendous change in their earnings.The women 
426 
 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
beneficiaries were able to cross the poverty line in urban areas of Gayeshpur 
and New Barrakpur towns with financial assistance from Swama Jayanti Sahari 
RozgarYojana (SJSRY). 
The study team observed, the three main factors which effect the 
community organizations/structures most namely conducive Politico-
Administrative milieu, the average size of Neighbourhood Groups (NHGs) for 
effective devaluation of power and uninterrupted, steady and adequate flow of 
funds for sustainability of Community Organisation. With the incentive to 
key functionaries, Resident Community Volunteers (RCVs) and Community 
Organisers (COs) can play a crucial role in the society bringing major changes 
in quality leadership, capacity building, health care and literacy etc. were 
found in the focus towns. 
The team observed that the success of SJSRY programme depends on 
smooth flow of funds from Centre to State in respect of componentwise 
budget and finally the cooperation of the banks in the matters of release of 
financial Assistance. In a vast geographical area a rigid schematic approach 
may be counter productive. At the Centre level the Scheme need to be 
relooked as estimated by expert groups on urban poverty anomalies. The 
team further suggested that the system of releasing funds to Urban Local Bodies 
(ULB) from State Urban Development Agency (SUDA) should be changed for 
effective implementation of SJSRY programme. 
The role of Thrift and Credit Societies and Vocational Training in 
different trades have immense impact among the urban poor resulted major 
changes in skill formation/up-gradation, confidence building all focused 
towards self-reliance if they are linked with Community Development Society 
(CDS).The CDS initiative increases the depositor confidence and access to 
resources. If the revolving fund amount is increased these organizations can 
also finance most of the loans which banks rejected. The team also opined that 
industrial development and Banks have unfavourable attitude towards 
DWCUA groups and micro-enterprises. 
The team observed that spending Urban Wage Employment Programme 
(UWEP) funds seems to be the easiest. Its poverty reduction effects, on a 
sustainable basis, are the least. The involvement of community organizations 
also is often peripheral. Both these shortcomings 
427 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
can be, at best, partially removed by building income-generating assets and 
effective devolution of financial control over UWEP expenditures to the 
community organizations. 
In spite of various set back, the Government of West Bengal has done a 
commendable job in setting up meaningful community organizations. The 
State has also shown some flexibilities in order that maximum benefits are 
extended to the poor under the constraints imposed by schematic b udget and 
procedures. 
RAJASTHAN 
Estimates of urban poor: Comparison of three different sets of data 
base suggests huge inaccuracy in estimation of incidence of poverty and 
targeting under SJSRY. 
The study recommended estimates of urban poverty need to be 
revisited by using a more sensitive set of indicators that can assess 
vulnerability. 
SJSRY achievement at the State and in sampled cities: 
Achievements under the Programme have been low both for outreach and credit 
assistance, Community Structure formed under the Programme are largely at 
the city level without the basic building blocks (NHG & NHC) and have 
overlapping membership. 
The State needs to set a time frame within which it will achieve 
universal coverage. Survey data may be updated. Municipal capacity, both in 
terms of staff and their skill, needs to be enhanced. 
Profile of beneficiaries provided loans: More loans were disbursed in larger 
cities. Women, on an average, received larger loans. One fourth of the loan 
beneficiaries, had studied beyond matriculation and were ineligible for 
receiving credit under the Scheme. 
Erroneus targeting for loan is th e primary reason for fund leakage. 
Project staff were inappropriately qualified and lack training to handle the 
activities. 
Nature of credit assistance and repayment: Loan is provided both for 
capital cost and recurring expenses. Majority of people were repaying loans 
regularly, yet, loan release system by the banks remained low. 
State may develop a MIS system to keep track of loans and to hold 
quarterly meetings with bank officials to share data about loan recovery. 
Targeting: Though accuracy of targeting BPL families for credit 
assistance was high, the income estimates based on reported incomes are 
questionable. 
428 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Socio-economic survey by using participatory tools may be used for 
targeting. ULB staff must be trained. Surveys need to be regularly updated. 
Overlapping schemes, targeting the same set of communities, with different 
rates of subsidy need to be merged. 
Training for self entrepreneurship: Training component has been weak 
due to poor utilisation of capacity building efforts. 
State needs to clearly articulate its strategy for capacity building 
through private sector participation, increasing training potential of small cities 
and developing an MIS to ensure better targeting and follow up of 
training/credit assistance. 
Urban Wage Employment Programme: Very few works have been 
undertaken under the wage employment. Wage employment is an intermittent 
activity with cycles of employment and unemployment and is unable to make a 
sustainable impact on poverty. 
UWEP needs a clear startegy: ULBs need to change. Civil work 
contracting norms and ensure greater transparency. Wage employment must be 
linked with skill training. 
Community Development Societies: CDS was not seen as a means of 
women's empowerment and civil society partners were not engaged in the 
process of CDS formation. Lack of involvement of officials in community 
organisation and low priority given to development programmes was the 
reason for the poor success of the programme. 
Officials engaged for organizing community activities must have 
appropriate skills and aptitude. CDS groups may be reformed at the 
settlement level with NHGs and NHCs and leadership amongst women may be 
nurtured. 
thrift and Credit Societies: None of theT&C Groups have provided credit 
to members for addressing personal emergencies, T&Cs, CDS and DWCUA 
Groups overlapped with common membership reducing further coverage under 
the programme. 
Programme officers need to clearly understand the purpose behind T&C 
Group formation. Matching grant provision needs to be dispensed with as it 
leads to unsustainable groups. Savings groups must be brought together to 
address small emergency needs. 
Development of Women and Children in the Urban Areas (DWCUA): 
Only a few DWCUA groups were found indicative of a dismal 
429 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
success rate. Reasons for poor performance under DWCUA were: lack of 
community confidence in working together, lack of awareness on choice of 
enterprise, lack of skills in marketing and delay in release of funds from the 
banks. 
DWCUA groups organised on a spatial or common interest networks would 
be useful as confidence building measures. Problems regarding release of 
funds need to be sorted out by discussing the matter with the banks. 
Banks: Procedure of sanctioning loans was tedious. Delay in release of funds 
by banks due to time lag in release of subsidy to banks. Banks officials feel that 
the scheme lacks teeth for loan recovery. 
Bank confidence can be enhanced through peer pressure for loan 
recovery. State must take initiative to resolve banking problr- is. 
Capacity of ULB functionaries: Capacity of ULB  dictionaries was low 
both in terms of required staff, qualifications and training. 
Persons with suitable qualifications must be deployed. All officials must 
be provided training. Sufficient number of community organizers must be 
inducted into the Programme. 
Involvement of NGOs: Smaller cities do-not have NGOs to support 
training. 
NGO participation must be encouraged under the Programme. 
Monitoring of Progra mme Implementation: None of the 
municipalities have computerized the information. Monitoring is generally done 
by the ULBs along with the banks officials once in a month. 
There is a need to computerize the data base and develop a MIS to keep 
track of loans and impact assessments. 
UTTAR PRADESH 
Recommendations: 
 Based on the responses received from various respondents (SUDA/ DUDA 
officials, Members of NHGs, NHCs and CDSs. Bank officials etc.) and 
our own observations in the field, the following recommendations 
have been made: 
430 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
• Issue of bribery needs immediate attention. During the formal 
interviews/contacts, the magnitude of the problem did not appear to be 
that grave as we came to know through informal dicussions. Strong 
measures have to be instituted to detect and punish malpractices like 
bribery. 
• For Poverty Alleviation Programmes to have impact in reducing/ 
removing poverty, there is a need for regular monitoring of 
programmes by independent bodies (those who are not involved in the 
implementation). 
• Proper use of funds and material benefits given to beneficiaries under 
any programme must be ensure to make the programme successful. 
• The training courses offered under USEP need to be tailored in 
accordance with the local situations. More emphasis should be given 
on practical training under these courses. These courses should also 
include basic concepts on financial management and marketing. 
• Efforts must be taken to maintain the Management Information 
System (MIS) at the community level, as the town is the focal point at 
which all urban development programmes are being implemented. 
Functionaries at the grass root level and those who are responsible to 
maintain records and registered need to be oriented from time to time. 
Staff should be equipped with hi-tech ways and means for better 
maintenance of records and effective monitoring of the programmes. 
• Efforts must be made to involve Non-Governmental Organisations 
(NGOs) in the Urban Development Programmes to ensure wider 
outreach. 
• For wage employment programmes, labour rates need to be reviewed more 
realistically and in a differentiated manner based on local specific 
market situations. Involvement of contractors for engaging labour needs 
to be looked into. 
431 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
• Delays in the release of funds should be strictly controlled, 
particularly for construction work, as it slows down the progress, 
causes cost escalation and affects the quality of the end product. 
• Some mechanism must be developed to put all details regarding 
programmes and activities to be undertaken on the notice boards of the 
BUDA in time and on regular basis to make the community aware and 
avail of the benefits. 
• There is a need for watch out for identifying beneficiaries under 
different programme in accordance with the laid-out guidelines of the 
Ministry. All pros and cons of each and every programme need to be 
explained to the community. 
• As part of the programme, the money spent on conveyance by RCV 
and Member of NHGs, NHCs and CDSs should be reimbursed, only then 
the programmes will be promoted. 
• There must be provision of honorarium for CDS Members so that they 
can be motivated for active participation. 
• Under self-employment programme, the training component is weak, as only 
one out of 5 beneficiaries reported to have received any training. It is, 
therefore, recommended that due emphasis should be given to the 
training of beneficiaries. 
• Implemented should ensure that all beneficiaries should get toolkit either 
free of cost or on subsidized rates after they satisfactorily complete the 
training. 
• Some proper mechanism/channels should be developed for marketing 
the produce of beneficiaries so that they would get maximum profit. 
• Hardly 5 per cent of beneficiaries reported functioning of Thrift and 
Credit Societies in their area. It is suggested that due emphasis should 
be given by NHGs to establish these societies seeing their importance in 
the successful implementation of the programme. 
• The programme lacks in sustainability. So, there is a promising need 
of developing some mechanism for the sustainability of the programme.

       Proposal from Chhattisgarh for drinking water project in Raipur 
2061. SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received a proposal for Rs. 58 crores in 
May-June, 2001 for drinking water project in Raipur (Chhattisgarh); 
(b) whether the amount has not been sanctioned, so far, causing lot of 
hardship to the people of Raipur; and 
(c) if so, by when this amount demanded by the State Government will be 
sanctioned? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Water supply being a State subject, it is the responsibility of 
State Governments to plan, implement, operate and maintain water supply 
facilities and make adequate provision of funds for this purpose. However, in 
order to supplement the efforts of the State Governments for providing water 
supply facilities in towns having population less than 20,000 (as per 1991 Census), 
this Ministry is implementing a Centrally sponsored Accelerated Urban Water 
Supply Programme (AUWSP) wherein Central assistance is provided to the State 
Governments on 50:50 matching basis. Since Raipur city is having population 
more than 20,000 as per 1991 Census, it cannot be considered under AUWSP. 
The State Government was advised to finance the project for Raipur City out of the 
funds provided by the Planning Commission under the State Plan and/or by taking 
loans from financial institutions like Life Insurance Corporation/Housing and 
Urban Development Corporation.

and National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), 18 Urban 
Co-operative Banks and 3 District Central Co-operative Banks were involved in 
irregularities during the period January, 2001 to June, 2002. These banks are 
likely to incur financial loss of Rs.1357.69 crores and Rs.208.03 crores 
respectively. In view of these irregularities, RBI and NABARD have initiated 
various measures. These include requiring the Registrars of Co-operative

†*340.  SHRI RAJIV RAN JAN            
SINGH'LALAN':                                            
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the report issued by 
World Bank in May, 2002 with regard to water management in India; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact that it has been mentioned In the said report that as 
a result of flaws in water management an annual loss of Rs. 74,730 crores is being 
suffered as per 1994-95 prices; and 
(c) if so, what is Government's reaction in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) to (c) The World Bank in one of its reports entitled "Initiating and 
Sustaining Water Sector Reforms: a Synthesis* published in 1999 had opined that 
there were certain shortcomings in the water resources management in the country, such 
as emphasis on development of water resources instead of its efficient management, 
need for comprehensive basin-wise management of water resources, absence of 
conjunctive use of surface and ground wafer, lack of concerns for quality and quantity 
aspects of water and non resolution of contentious issues of allocation of 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
465 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
inter-state river waters. In this context, the report mentions estimated costs .of 
inaction in monetary terms in respect of water pollution, soil degradation, and 
revenue deficit in the form of low water rates and power subsidy in agriculture. 
The National Water Policy of 1987 which has largely guided the water 
resources development in the country already addresses the inadequacies mentioned 
in the World Bank report. Importance of efficient and sustainable development of 
water resources, integrated development of surface and ground water through 
conjunctive use, program for improvement in quality of water and its efficient 
utilization has been emphasized in the National Water Policy. State Governments 
are managing their water resources under these policy provisions. The imperatives 
of agricultural development and the sensitivities/compulsions of socio-
economic disparities have guided the policies of the States on subsidising the 
agricultural and power sector. As such the alleged costs of inaction, as 
estimated in the World Bank report are not on sound footing. 
The revised National Water Policy 2002 further broadens the 
framework for improved and sustainable development and management of water 
resources.

The pace of investment in the Indian Industries has slowed down. Studies 
conducted by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Centre for Monitoring 
Indian Economy (CMIE) have identified lack of aggregate 
497 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
demand as the primary cause for industr ial slowdown and the recent fall in 
investment both in public and private sectors.The other factors, structural and 
cyclical, responsible for slowdown are: 
(i) Operation of Investment and business cycles, 
(ii) Inherent adjustment lags of corporate restructuring, 
(iii) Lack of both consumer and investment demand, 
(iv) High real interest rate, 
(v) Infrastrucutre constraints, particularly, in power, 
(vi) Lack of reforms inland and labour markets, and 
(vii)   Economic slowdown in countries that are major trading partners of 
India, viz., USA, Japan and European Union. 
(c)TheTenth Five Year Plan is in the process of finalization. However, the 
Approach Paper for theTenth Five Year Plan approved by the National 
Development Council (NDC) indicates that in order to achieve the target of 8 
per, cent growth in Gross Domestic Product (GDP), the industrial sector will 
have to grow over 10 perceri|3rtir#al terms. This represents a major acceleration 
from its past performance', which has to take place in an environment that will 
be significantly different from the past. First, industry will have to face much 
stronger international competition, as Indian domestic market is now more 
open with Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) on imports having been removed 
with effect from April,2001. Secondly, the relative role of the public sector will 
decline in the course of Tenth Plan as the incremental capacities will be mainly 
in the private sector, in addition to the fact that disinvestment converts many 
of the existing public sector enterprises to non-government enterprises. 
The Government has taken several policy initiatives to accelerate the 
pace of investment and create conducive atmosphere for investment. These steps 
have been targeted to improve competitiveness of Indian industry in general 
and to boost aggregate demand, improve infrastructure base, upgrade technology, 
and encourage Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) 
498 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
flows and rationalize tax structure. Some such steps taken recently are briefly 
mentioned below: 
• Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion (DIPP) has entrusted a 
study to assess global competitiveness of capital goods sector to an 
organization of international repute. 
• Medium Term Export Strategy for 2002—2007 was announced 
emphasizing the importance of maintaining appropriate real effective 
exchange rate coupled with lower duties for inputs needed for exports.-
These include transparent and comprehensive schemes of tax 
reimbursement, comprehensive VAT system at every level, rebating 
service tax besides lower customs and excise duties for major inputs 
needed for exports, which can minimise the need for duty drawback. 
• Sector-wise strategies to boost production for exports in key sectors, 
which include engineering/electronic/electrical and allied, textiles, gems 
& jewellery, chemicals & allied sector, have also been announced in 
the MediumTerm Export Strategy. 
• To improve operating environment of the companies, Companies Act 
has been amended to allow buy-back of Shares by the companies. 
• Power sector reforms have received a boost in pursuance of the centre's 
decision to provide grants equal to the amount by which States have 
been able to reduce their power sector deficits.The States of Haryana, 
Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh have been able to reduce losses in the 
past couple of years. While Haryana is expected to emerge with cash 
profits in 2001-2002, Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh have reduced 
their power sector deficits. These three States will now be eligible for 
matching grant under the Accelerated Power Development and 
Reform Programme (APDRP). 
• The draft Electricity Bill has been introduced in the Parliament for 
facilitating comprehensive power sector reforms.

Speeding up of container movements 
2111. SHRI R.R GOENKA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleasea to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that inordinate delay in handling containers at ports 
during the last few weeks has brought exports to a virtual standstill, inasmuch as 
exports worth Rs. 250 crores and imports goods worth Rs. 450 crores are 
reportedly stuck at various container depots and customs; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the short term/long term ste oc taken to speed up container 
movements to protect and promote international trade? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHfll RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b)The value of 
export and import consignments stuck up for past few weeks due to delay in 
handling of containers is not available. However, there was delay in handling 
of containers at Jawaharlal Nehru Po rt (JNP) and Nhava Sheva International 
ContainerTerminal (NSICT) due to container handling problems, heavy rain in 
Maharashtra and Gujarat and, breaches in Palghar-Vaitarana section of 
Western Railways. 
(c) In order to speed up container movements following measures have 
been taken up: 
(i)    Two additional lines were operationalised temporarily for 10 days 
by Container Corporation of India (CONCOR); 
(ii) Additional container handling equipments and rakes have been made 
available; 
(iii) JNPT has taken in principle decision to take over Inland 
Container Depot operations on rail lines 6 and 8; and 
(iv) CONCOR's proposal to handle ICD rakes designated for Nagpur 
and Hyderabad ICDs at their Dronagiri Node rail terminal has 
been accepted by JNPT and the same has been operationalised.

FDI in Plantation Sector 
2112. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to refer to answer to Unstarred 
Question 631 given in the Rajya Sabha on 23rd July, 2002 and state: 
(a) whether FDI has also been permitted in other plantations; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the reaction of the foreign owned tea majors to the opening of the tea 
sector to FDI? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a) No, Sir. FDI up to 100% is 
permitted only in tea sector, including tea plantations. 
(b) Unlike tea plantations, which are facing the problem of aging bushes 
and also have a significant presence of foreign companies, from the very 
beginning, which have been allowed to carry on business under FERA, subject 
to a minimum of 26% Indian participation in the equity capital, the other 
plantations like rubber, coffee, etc., have a totally different industry structure where 
the need for FDI has not yet been felt. 
(c) No formal feedback on the new policy has been received.

2120. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the ICICI Bank has decided to target agricultural financing; 
(b) if so, whether they have identified it as one of the new growth areas 
in future; 
(c) whether the main aim of the bank is to reach out to the farmers and 
provide finance to them directly; 
(d) if so, what are the main steps the ICICI has taken in this regard; 
(e) whether any schemes have been prepared for the agricultural 
financing; and 
(f) if so, by when they are likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) and 
(b) ICICI Bank has reported that it feels that agriculture is an important sector 
with immense potential for growth in the near future. Accordingly, it has 
commenced focusing on the opportunities in agricultural lending by 
constituting a dedicated Agri business group, which has the capability to 
structure specific products for rural finance. 
(c) to (f) ICICI Bank has further repo rted that it is using a sector 
specific approach with key focus on th e dairy, crop prod uction, poultry, 
agricultural infrastructure, plantations, horticulture, food processing etc. and 
has facilitated crop specific assistance to the farmers through a structure 
financing concept called the Farmer Service Centres (FSCs). The crop 
assistance provided through FSCs is as follows: 
• Providing quality inputs like fertilizers, pesticides, seeds and credit 
• Soil testing facility through tie-ups with soil testing laboratories 
• Extension services to the farmers regarding planting, crop 
production practices and post harvest handling 
• Crop monitoring through extension agents and timely advice 
towards the use of inputs 
527 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
• Integrated pest control techniques 
• Information regarding the market and mandi prices 
• Procurement of crop through FSC and tie-up with marketers for 
sale of produce. 
To extend credit to the farmers, ICICI Bank has associated with 
extension service providers, input companies marketing companies, NGOs and 
Sugar companies. ICICI Bank has already taken up pilot funding programmes 
for financing the farmers through these intermediate channels. The pilot programmes 
have been conducted in different geographic locations across the country and in 
crops like paddy, wheat, groundnut, fruits and vegetables, cotton etc. The success 
of the pilot programmes demonstrated last year has given an impetus to ICICI 
Bank's direct agriculture lending programmes and they are being scaled up 
with the corporate partners across the country.

operative Bank nexus detected in December, 2001;

Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that while reviewing the 
transactions in Government securities undertaken through Constituent 
Subsidiary General Ledger (CSGL) accounts maintained with commercial banks, 
it was noticed that large volume of transactions in Government securities had 
been undertaken through these CSGL accounts between broker entities and

securities by banks were fraudulent in nature and were in violation of RBI 
guidelines/instructions. 
(c) With a view to eliminate the nexus between the brokers and the banks, 
RBI has taken vaious steps. Some of these are: 
 Issue of instructions indicating that transactions in Government 
securities should not be undertaken with brokers as counter parties; 
 All purchase/sale transactions in Government securities by banks 
should necessarily be through SGL account with RBI 
539

or CSGL accounts with designated agencies or dematerialised account with 
depositories; 
 No further transactions in Government securities by banks should be 
undertaken in physical form with any broker;

 The entities maintaining the CSGL/designated funds accounts are required to 
ensure availability of clear funds in the designated funds accounts for purchases 
and of sufficient securities in the CSGL account for sales before putting through 
the transactions; 
Taking further measures, to beef up the supervisory and internal control system 
in Co-operative banks through strict audit of investment transactions of all 
State and District Central Cooperative Banks.

thousand crores the credit to people by these banks stand fts. 8 thousand crores 
i.e. 23%;

banks, the credit-deposit ratio in Bihar does not improve; and

COMFANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) and (b) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) have reported that the aggregate deposits and 
gross Bank credit of public sector banks (State Bank of India and its associate 
banks and nationalised banks) was Rs.25,576.70 crore and Rs.5468.09 crore 
respectively as on 31 st March, 2002. Accrodingly Credit Deposit (CD) Ratio 
works out to 21.4 per cent. 
(c) and (d) A Special Task Force was set up consequent to a State Level 
Bankers' Committee (SLBC) meeting held on 7th January, 1999 wherein 
serious concern over the declining Credit Deposit (CD) ratio in Bihar was 
expressed. The task force was asked to look into the industry related problems 
in Bihar. A Sub-Committee was accordingly formed to 
543

measures to increase CD Ratio.The progress in implementation of action points 
that emerged from the study shows that the banks have been making all

infrastructure facilities, development of core sector projects, large and medium 
industries entrepreneurial initiatives, credit absorption capacity of the State,

Overdraft of State Government 
2141. SHRI KAILASH JOSHI: Will  the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the limit of overdraft a State can draw, State-wise; 
(b) the names and details of overdraft drawn by States during the last 
two years; 
(c) whether Government propose to set up a panel to reform RBI's 
present practice with regard to overdraft limits by States; and 
 (d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND  
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) Overdraft of 
States with Reserve Bank of India are governed by the Ways and Means 
Advance and Overdraft Regulation Scheme of the RBI, as revised from time to 
time. Presently there is no limit on the amount of overdraft that a State can 
draw. 
(b) The transaction between a State and the RBI is conducted as per an 
agreement between the two. Since, it is a matter of relationship between the 
banker and the client (between the Reserve Bank of India and the State 
Government), such information is not published/made public by Govt, of India. 
(c) and (d)The existing Ways and Means Advance and Overdraft 
Regulation Scheme of the Bank is due for review in March 2003. A decision 
has been taken by RBI to form a Group to review the Scheme. 
Domestic savings 
2142. SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a decline in the domestic savings rate from 25 to about  
550 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
22-23 per cent of GDP will have adverse impact on the economic growth of the 
country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the targeted growth rate of 7 to 8 per cent will 
not be achieved without insuring domestic savings at 32 per cent of GDP; 
(c) what are the new productive saving instruments planned by 
Government that would assure a reasonable rate of return to householders and 
thereby encourage demestic savings; and 
(d) whether any tax free-saving instruments, beyond those 
indicated in the budget are contemplated, if so, whether these would 
be indicated? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRIANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) Domestic 
savings rate measured in terms of gross demestic savings as a proportion of GDP 
at current market prices improved from 23.2 per cent in 1999-2000 to 23.4 
per cent in 2000-01. 
(b) As per the Approach Paper to the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002—
07) approved by the National Development Council, given an incremental 
capital output ratio of around 4.08, annual average growth in real GDP of 8 
per cent may be achieved through the gross domestic investment rate of 32.6 
per cent of GDP at current market prices, which would be financed by 
external capital flows amounting to 2.8 per cent of GDP and gross domestic 
savings of 29.8 per cent of GDP. 
(c) and (d) The Finance Minister, while announcing the 
Supplementary Demands for Grants for 2002-03, has proposed the following 
measures which would encourage the growth of domestic savings: 
(i) Increase in deduction under Section 80L to Rs. 15,000 comprising Rs. 
12,000 for income from specified investments and Rs. 3000 on 
interest on Government securities. 
551 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
(ii) Increase in the limit in respect of dividend income upto Rs. 2500 
received from each company or a mutual fund for tax deduction 
at source for senior citizens and investors. 
(iii)    Life insurance premia to be totally exempt from serivce tax. 
(iv) The Government propose to shortly offer a new scheme of tax-
free bond with enhanced monetary ceiling which will have an 
interest rate of 7 per cent and a maturity period of 6 years.

CRISIL rating oflDBI 
2151. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will  the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that CRISIL rating of IDBI has come down from 
AAA+ to AA+ in about two years; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken to improve the credibility of IDBI? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) IDBI has 
reported that CRISIL re vised the rating for IDBI bonds and Certificate of 
Deposits from "AAA" to "AA+" during July 2001. 
(b) According to the rating rationale of CRISIL, the rating revision is 
attributed to decline in profitability of IDBI due to a combination of asset 
quality problems and contraction in spreads and non-fructification of the earlier 
indicated recapitalisation plan. 
(c) To address the concerns of the rating agency, steps have been taken 
by IDBI to improve the asset quality, profitability and further strengthening 
its fundamentals. The steps include measures to reduce borrowing cost, 
administrative cost of IDBI and diversification of asset base in favour of short 
term loans with higher yield. 
Vigilance of RBI over Private Banks 
2152. SHRI NANDIYELLAIAH: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any constant vigilance over the functioning of 
578 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Private Banks and Private financial Institutions by the Reserve Bank of India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the reasons for upgradation of Charminar Bank of Hyderabad to a 
Multi-State Scheduled Bank despite severe financial irregularities found by 
Reserve Bank of India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) to (c) In 
terms of the provisions of Section 35 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) conducts Annual Financial Inspection of Banks. 
The findings of RBI's inspection report are taken up with the banks' 
management for taking remedial steps to ensure that the irregularities 
observed do not recur. The compliance of the inspection report is monitored 
by RBI. 
The Non Banking Financial Institutions (NBFCs) are regulated and 
supervised by the RBI under the provisions of Chapter-Ill and Chapter-V of the 
RBI Act, 1934. RBI's supervision of NBRCs comprises on-site and off-site 
inspection, effective market intelligence network and submission of reports by 
the auditors of NBFCs. 
(d) RBI has reported that the Charminar Co-operative Urban Bank Ltd., 
Hyderabad had applied for Multi-State Status in 1999 and since the bank's 
financial position as on 31st March, 1999 met all the parameters fixed in this 
regard, RBI has issued 'No Objection Certificate' for extension of area operation of 
the bank from Mumbai in Maharashtra to the Central Registrar of Co-operative 
Societies, New Delhi. The Registration of the bank under the Multi-State Co-
operative Societies Act, 1984 has, however, been cancelled by the Central 
Registrar of Co-operative Societies, New Delhi vide orders dated 19th June, 
2002.

2157. SHRI K.B. KRISHNAMURTHY: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are fully seized of the ramifications of the recent 
hometrade.com Urban Cooperative Ba nk involving Government securities 
and if so, summary of the investigations made so far; 
(b) the reasons for the Reserve Bank of India not acting on hindsight after 
the Madhavpura Urban Cooperative Bank scam and other Pune based Urban 
Cooperative Bank scams, to prevent the hometrade.com scam; and 
(c) whether Government would probe the questionable role of the RBI in 
permitting Urban Cooperative Banks to continue perpetrating such frauds in 
regular succession? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
Government and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) are fully seized of the 
ramification of the recent irregularities in securities transactions undertaken by 
certain Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs). RBI has reported that while reviewing 
these transactions it was revealed that these UCBs are likely to incur financial 
loss of Rs. 170.64 crore as Home Trade and certain other brokers did not deliver 
the Government securities to the UCBs even though the banks had parted with 
funds to these brokers for purchase of Government securities. The scrutiny 
also revealed the following irregularities: 
Routing transactions through individual brokers in excess of the 
prudential norms of 5%; 
582 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Non-observance of delivery versus payment mechanism; 
Undertaking transactions with brokers as counter parties; 
Undertaking simultaneous transactions i.e. sell and purchase with 
the same broker; 
Laxity in internal control system, etc. 
Transaction in Government securities in physical form in violation of 
the RBI instructions. 
(b) and (c) RBI has laid down detailed guidelines under which all 
transactions in Government securities are to be undertaken only through SGL 
account where available but these banks undertook transactions in the physical 
mode and the physical delivery of the securities were not insured.These 
violations had come to the light in course of regular statutory inspections or as a 
follow up on off-site surveillance. These transactions were manifestly fraudulent 
transactions and did not reflect in any way on adequacy of regulatory guidelines. 
Further, the violations were not of the type observed in the case of Madhavpura 
Mercantile Co-operative Bank. In view of the manifest fraudulent transaction in 
violation of its guidelines and to forestall any further damage, RBI has taken 
several actions both on the policy level and against the individual banks to 
ensure that the irregularities of the type observed do not recur.

Details of Transfer Policy of Oil PSUs 
1. The postings/transfers in the oil PSUs are based on specific 
organizational needs and individuals requirements and also as per the 
terms and conditions of service in the company. 
2. Non-officer category of employees are not generally transferred. 
3. As far as possible transfers are carried out during January-March every 
year. Normally no mid term transfers are made except in the case of 
exceptional organizational requirements. 
4. Normal tenure at a location is 3 to 5 years and the officers are not usually 
transferred in a period of less than two years. 
5. Rotational transfers of employees working in sensitive and direct public 
dealing positions for more than 3 years. 
6. The main objectives of transfers are exigencies of work, manning of 
hard locations, career developoment and requirement of specialised 
knowledge. 
7. Choice/preferabel postings on transfer from the hardship locations such as 
North Eastern Region/J and K. 
8. Where officers' spouse is also employee in the same PSU, both are 
posted at the same location, as far as possible. 
9. Special consideration is given to the physically handicapped officers. 
 
10. On promotion of non-executives to executive cadre employees are 
transferred from one work centre to another to enhance their 
experience/job profile. 
11. Except for administrative requiremen ts, Officers retiri ng in the next 
three years or less are not transferred from their existing locations.

2188.   DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM

610

Shri Mathew Panickar which appeared in the Week dated 30th June, 2002 to the

on an average, Dollar 1 to Dollar 1.5 more than countries of Europe and

differential price removed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM

Compensation to the oustees in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh 
2222. SHRIMANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether cash compensation is being given as an alternative to land-
based rehabilitation to the SSP dam oustees in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh;

(c) if so, what are the details of the reasons for such gross change? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c)The land 
based Resettlement and Rehabilitation (R&R) policy as stipulated by 
Narmada Water DisputesTribunal (NWDT) Award is being implemented by the 
concerned State Governments namely Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat. 
No cash compensation is being given by Government of Gujarat in lieu of 
land. In case of Madhya Pradesh, the Project Affected Families (PAFs) 
entitled to land for land are being offered land, as per provision contained in 
NWDT Award. In the event, if PAFs are unwilling to take the land offered by 
the State Government and give their choice consent for cash in lieu of offered 
land to purchase the land of their own choice, then only cash is being offered by 
Government as per set procedure for purchase of land by the oustee himself. 
The provision of cash in lieu of land to the Madhya Pradesh PAFs, 
keeping in view their choice, is an additional liberalized R&R package by 
Government of Madhya Pradesh and is over and above the NWDT Award.

hydro projects.This is aimed at reduction in time and cost over runs

introduced. This facilitates thorough preparation of DPRs so as to 
minimize possibilities of geological surprises with land acquisition and 
proper development of infrastructure including roads and bridges being done 
in parallel after establishment of feasibility and commercial viability of

Pension to 1965 and 1971 war-widows 
*351.   SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: 
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the women widowed during the 1965 and 1971 
wars have petitioned against the discriminatory pension rules as reported in 
the Times of India dated 13th July, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government propose to remove various anomalies in the 
pension rules and provide other facilities to war widows; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
to (d) Some petitions have been receiv ed requesting for rationalization of 
Liberalised Special Family Pension in respect of war widows of pre 1.1.1996 
cases of Armed Forces personnel.The demand of the war-widows of 1965 and 1971 
wars relates to modified parity in pensionary benefits given to pre 1996 war 
widows. Their demand is that the liberalized family pension and other benefits 
granted to war widows remarried after 1.1.1996 should also be granted to widows 
remarried before 1.1.1996. 
2. The war widows are entitled to liberalized family pension at the rate- 
of last pay drawn by the deceased at the time of his death. In pursuance of the 
recommendation of the Fifth Pay Commission, the liberalized family pension 
of war widows prior to 1.1.1996 has also been revised to the minimum of the 
new pay scale introduced w.e.f. 1.1.1996 provided their consolidated liberalized 
family pension is not more than the minimum of the new pay scale. 
3.The demand of the 1965 and 1971 war-widows who got remarried prior to 
1.1.1996, is for extending to them the benefits of liberalized family pension given 
to the widows who got remarried after 1.1.1996. According to the orders in force 
before 1.1.1996, the liberalized family pension granted to a war-widow was 
converted into ordinary family pension from the date following the date of her 
remarriage except in case of remarriage with real brother of the deceased 
personnel.This order has been modified to provide

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
that the war-widows remarrying after 1.1.1996 can continue to draw

revised orders have prospective effect from 1.1.1996.

Power shortage in the country 
*353. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Wi ll the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the power deficit in the country, State-wise, during last three years; 
(b) the reasons for power shortage in the country; 
(c) the additional power generation targeted and achieved during the Eighth 
and Ninth Five Year Plan; and 
(d) the steps taken to solve the problem of the power deficit during the 
Tenth Five Year Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) State-
wise power supply position in the country during 1999-2000, 2000-01 and 
2001-02 is given in the Statement enclosed {see below) 
(b)The main reasons for shortage of power in the country are: 
(i) Growth in demand for power outpacing the growth in generation-low 
capacity addition during 9th Plan. 
(ii) Non-availability of adequate inter-regional tie lines restricting 
export of power from surplus region to deficit region. 
(iii) Inadequate strengthening of sub-transmission and distribution 
network due to inadequate funding by power utilities. 
(iv) Shortage of peaking power in the grid. 
(v) Low Plant Load Factor (PLF) of some of the thermal generating units. 
(vi) Inadequate inflow into the hydro reservoirs affecting hydel 
generation. 
653 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
(c) The capacity addition during Eighth Plan was 16423 MW as against 
the target of 30538 MW and the capacity addition during Ninth Plan was 
19019 MW as against a target of 40245 MW. 
(d) The following steps are being taken to improve the generation and 
availability of power in the country: 
(i) A capacity addition of around 41,100 MW has been targeted for 10th 
Five Year Plan. 
(ii) Early stabilization of newly commissioned units and overall 
increase in Plant Load Factor of thermal units. 
(iii) Strengthening/Augmentation of Reduction inTransmission and 
Distribution losses. Funds are being provided for undertaking 
schemes for transmission and distri bution systems to States under 
the accelerated Power Development & Reforms Programme. 
(iv) Demand side management and Promoting energy efficiency and 
conservation measures. 
(v) Disbursement of loans by the Power Finance Corporation for 
improving operation and maintenance of thermal power stations. 
(vi) Enhancement of inter-state and inter-regional power transfer by 
strengthening of inter regional transmission links and finally 
leading to formation of the National grid. 
(vii) Exploitation of hydro potential at a faster pace. 
According to 16th Electric Power Survey brought out by the Central 
Electricity Authority, an additional capacity of about 1,07,000 MW is 
required to meet the demand of power by 2012 AD. For the 10th Five year Plan 
(2002-07), the target for capacity addition of around 41,000 MW has been 
planned.The experience of the poor performance in capacity addition during 9th 
Plan, was kept in View while fixing targets for the 10th Plan. During the 9th 
Plan, there was over dependence on 
654 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
capacity.addition by the Independent Power Producers (IPPs), which did not 
materialize as these projects could not attain financial closure on account of 
poor financial health of the State Electricity Boards (SEBs). Hence, for the 
10th Plan, 22830 MW is expected from the central sector, approx. 11,150 
MW from the State sector and around 7120 MW from the Private Sector. A 
National Conference was held on the 8th and 9th of July, 2002 at New Delhi 
to ascertain whether the targets were realistic and whether they could be 
attained. This conference was attended by the State Power Secretaries and 
Chairmen of SEBs and in their presence, each listed project was reviewed and 
critical constraints were identified. After detailed deliberations, it was agreed 
that this target of 41,000 MW was realistic considering the fact that about 
19,000 MW is already under construction and another 8500 MW has the 
requisite approvals. An encouraging factor is that The outlay for the 10th 
Plan has been enhanced by 214% vis-a-vis the 9th Plan Outlay. This would 
ensure that adequate funds would be available for the capacity addition 
programme. One of the major reasons for poor capacity addition has been the 
inability of the SEBs/ utilities to raise required finances. A number of steps 
have been initiated to reforms and restructure the sector to make it financially 
viable. 
The Government of India has signed Memorandum of Understanding 
(MOU)/Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) with twenty-two States. These 
reflect the joint commitment of the Centre and the States to undertake 
reforms in a time bound manner. The State Government's commitment in 
these MOUs include setting up of the State Electricity Regulatory 
Commission, 100% metering of 11 KV feeders, effective energy audit, 
identification and elimination of power theft and attainment of commercial 
viability in distribution. Government of India has committed its support 
through additional allocation of power from Central Generating Stations and 
financial assistance for strengthening of sub-transmission and distribution as 
well as for renovation and modernization of power plants. 
Government have launched the Accelerated Power Development 
655 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
and Reforms Programme (APDRP) to assist the States in improving their sub-
transmission/distribution system in identified circles and to provide incentive 
grants linked to the bridging of the gap between cost of supply and average 
revenue per unit. Twelve State Electricity Regulatory Commissions have 
passed tariff orders, which reflect a trend towards tariff rationalization. 
In addition, measures for Energy Conservation, Demand Side 
Management, Renovation and Modernisation, encouragement of captive 
power plants and reduction of transmission and distribution losses (including 
control and elimination of theft) are expected to further improve the 
availability of power. Besides, the proposed National Grid would eliminate 
the transmission hurdles, which are faced in transmitting electricity from 
surplus areas like Eastern Region. The Draft Electricity Bill, 2001 proposes to 
allow open access to consumers in a phased manner as may be allowed by 
regulatory Commission. The Regulatory Commissions may allow open 
access without eliminating cross subsidies by way of imposing a surcharge on 
transmission/wheeling on the consumers opting for open access. 
In order to bring International investors, power majors and institutions face 
to face, Confederation of Indian Industries and Federation of Indian Chambers of 
Commerce & Industry in association with Ministry of Power, five International 
Conferences and Business Meets were organized.These were in the fields of 
transmission, energy management; distribution reforms; non-fossil fuel 
generation; fossil fuel generation and optimization of existing capacity. 
The draft Electricity Bill, 2001 which is under consideration of 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Energy, provides for stringent 
penalties against theft of power. States of Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, 
Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh have enacted/promulgated stringent anti-theft 
legislation. 
It is expected that with the effective implementation of reforms, 
commercial viability would be achieved and the confidence of investors in power 
sector will improve.

*354. SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Power Trading Corporation of India Limited has started 
negotiations with the Nepal Electricity Authority for import of surplus power from 
the neighbouring country; 
(b) if so, the outcome of the talks held; 
(c) the total import of power made  during 2-01-2002 by PTC from 
Nepal; and 
(d) the agreement reached for import of power during the year 2002-2003? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) and 
(b)Yes, Sir.The first meeting between PowerTrading Corporation of India Ltd. 
(PTC) and the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) was held at Kathmandu in 
September, 2001 for discussing the issues relating to import of surplus power 
from Nepal to India. Decisions taken in the meeting on the various issues are as 
under: 
Existing operational and metering arrangements will continue. 
PTC will be responsible for all commercial issues relating to wheeling and 
revenue realization on the Indian side. 
Nepal will be able to export 100-150 M W of power after commissioning of 
Kaligandaki Hydro-electric Power Project (144 MW) to India during the months 
May to October from 2002 to 2017. 
Further action is required to be taken by PTC and NEA on the 
following issues: 
Examination of the technical feasibility for importing power to India 
through the existing feeders in radial mode. For this, NEA would furnish the 
list of feeders on which it would export power and continue import of power. 
According priority to construction of 132 KV Butwal (Nepal)— 
Anandnagar (Uttar Pradesh) line. 
Examination of technical feasibility for synchronization of a generating 
station in Nepal to the Uttar Pradesh Grid in the Northern Region through a 
132 KV double circuit line for which NEA would furnish the system details.

Continuing exchange at the present tariff till the commercial terms are

Abandoned ship detected by coast guard 
2243. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of Defence be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the newsitem titled 
'Was abandoned Lebanese ship AL-Qaeda's getaway vehicle' published in the 
Hindustan Times, dated 9th July, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard and his reaction thereto; 
(c) whether the ship was detected within the maritime zone of India, and 
whether it indicate security lapse on the part of the concerned agency; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken to prevent recurrence of such lapses and to further 
strengthen the vigil on our coasts? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
to (d) A merchant ship reported sighting of an abandoned merchant ship 'MV 
Al Murtada' on 3rd July, 2002 in position 84 nautical miles west of-Ratnagiri 
(110 nautical miles south of Mumbai). Coast Guard Ship Vijaya was sailed to 
monitor the movements of the vessel and boarded her on 6th July, 2002 and 
subsequently anchored the ship about 5 nautical miles of Devgarh (155 nautical 
miles south of Mumbai). During the preliminary search of the vessel, two AK 47 
rifles with words "ALLAH" and "YUSUF" inscribed in Urdu were recovered. 
On further rummaging, 3 loaded magazines of AK 47 bore (74 rounds) were 
also recovered. An Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team of Navy also 
embarked the ship on 9th July, 2002 to sanitise the vessel of any explosives. 
None were found. As intimated by International Maritime Bureau the last owner 
of the ship is Mr. Assem Nidal Beaini, Lebanon. 
682 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Enquiries have revealed that the ship had crew of 16 members which included 
Somalians - 6, Syrians - 4, and Lebanese - 4 besides 4 Indians. It developed 
some snag in mid-sea during its journey from Somalia to Dubai and remained 
floating in mid-sea. On receiving an SOS from the ship, US ship 'Vicks Burg' 
came to their rescue and airlifted on 16th June, 2002 all the crew members to 
another vessel 'MV Stolet Spray' which was sailing towards Kandla Port. Finally, 
the latter ship berthed in Kandla on June 18/19,2002 and thereafter all the 
foreign crew members left for their respective countries via mumbai after 
completion of immigration formalities through local Shipping Agent at Kandla. All 
the four Indian crew members on board the vessel Al Murtada have been 
identified. 
The ship was not in the Maritime Zone of India when the incident 
occurred. But drifted into Indian waters after the crew was rescued by the US 
Naval ship and abandoned the vessel. 
There has been no security lapse. The surveillance and patrolling off the 
West coast is jointly done by the Indian Navy and Coast Guard. Besides, 
Indian Coast Guard has institutionalised a system wherein merchant ships 
transiting through the Indian maritime zones are encouraged to pass information in 
case any suspicious vessel is sighted.

Natural disasters in the country 
2265. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that India is becoming more and more 
prone to natural disasters; 
(b) if so, the details thereof during the last five years year-wise and State-
wise; 
(c) whether the country has well-knit forecasting systems and 
observational network to warm the authorities of the impending events; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the details of the disaster management machinery in operation to meet 
the national calamities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) and (b) On account of urbanization and population 
growth, the impact of natural disasters is felt to a larger extent. During the last five 
years, there have been two major disasters namely Super Cyclone, Orissa in 
October, 1999 and Gujarat earthquake in January, 2001 
700 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
besides the Chamoli earthquake in March, 1998 and the Gujarat cyclone in June 
1998. Floods and drought are a regular feature every year in one or the other part of 
the country. 
(c) and (d) Central Water Commission (CWC) in the Ministry of Water 
Resources is the nodal organisation for flood forecasting and warning and has 159 
flood forecasting stations in different parts of the country. India Meteorological 
Department (IMD) has also set up Flood Meteorological offices (FMOs) at 10 
locations to provide meteorological support to the CWC. For cyclones, IMD 
under the Ministry of Science & Technology is the nodal organisation and has 
established a full fledged National Cyclone Warning system which includes three 
area cyclone warning centres at Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai and the three 
cyclone warning centres at Bhubaneshwar, Vishakapatnam and Ahmedabad. 
IMD also maintains a Network of coastal radars and surface and upper air 
observatories along the coast line for observation and surveillance of tropical 
cyclones. In case of earthquakes, there is no scientific technique available in the 
world to forecast its occurrence with a reasonable degree of accuracy in regard to 
space, time and magnitude. However, the IMD has a countrywide network of 
50 siesmological observatories. 
(e) At the national level, Ministry of Home Affairs is the nodal Ministry for 
coordinating central efforts in case of natural (except drought) and man made 
disasters. The other Central Departments which provide emergency support 
functions are Ministry of Defence including Armed forces, Health, Rural 
Development Road Transport and Highways, Railways, Urban Development, 
Food & Public Distribution, Petroleum & Natural Gas, Power, Communication, 
Science &Technology etc.There is also an empowered Group of Ministers for

Contingency Fund.
