Proposal to include Dogri in the Eighth Schedule 
2276. MIRZA ABDUL RASHID: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to refer to reply to Unstarred Question 661 given in the Rajya 
Sabha on 6th March, 2002 and state: 
(a) whether Government propose to introduce a Bill, to include Dogri  
language in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, during the current session 
of Parliament; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
709 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) and (b) The text of this question refers to reply given 
on 6th March, 2002 to Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question No. 661. Perhaps the 
Hon'ble Member intended to refer to his Unstarred Question No. 2561 replied 
on the 17th April, 2002. 
At present demands for inclusion of as many as 32 more languages 
(including Dogri) in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution of India are 
pending with the Government.The Government have decided that a suitable criteria 
needs to be evolved for inclusion of more languages in the Eighth Schedule as no 
criteria has been laid down in the Constitution of India. 
The issue of evolving criteria for inclusion of more languages in the 
Eighth Schedule was referred to the "National Commission to Review the 
Working of the Constitution" for consideration.The National Commission has 
since submitted its report to the Government but the National Commission 
have not made any recommendations on this issue. Therefore, it has been decided 
by the Government to constitute a High Powered Body for laying down a 
criteria for inclusion of additional languages in the Eighth Schedule. The 
question of inclusion of more languages including Dogri in the Eighth Schedule 
would be considered in accordance with the criteria so evolved.

Uniform electricity tariff rates 
2300. SHRIMATISAVITA SHARDA: Wii; the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are contemplating to introduce 
uniform electricity tariff rates throughout the country; 
(b) if so, whether Government have so far taken any action in this 
regard; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) No, Sir. 
Consumer tariffs are required to be fixed by the State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) in the States where such Commissions have 
been set up under the Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) Act, 1998 or 
under the State Reform Acts. Where the SERCs have not been set up or are yet 
to become fully functional, tariffs are to be determined by the State Electricity 
Boards/State Electricity Departments/licensees. 
(b) In view of (a) above the question does not arise. 
(c) In view of (a) & (b) above the question does not arise.

2301. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister 
of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there have been protest against the power tariff revision at 
several places throughout India; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) Some categories of 
745 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
consumers including agricultural consumers do sometimes protest against the 
tariff increases decided by State Electricity Boards (SEBs)/State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) in some States. 
The National Development Council (NDC) appointed a Committee on 
Power chaired by Chief Minister of Maharashtra.The report submitted in 
September, 1994 recommended inter alia, that, 
— The State Government should adopt minimum All India 
Agricultural Tariffs as notified by Ministry of Power/Central 
Electricity Authority and also should agree to provide subsidy to the 
SEBs in a transparent manner to compensate for the losses, if any. 
— Subsidies to the agricultural consumers should be progressively phased 
out. 
Chief Ministers' Conference held in 1996 adopted a Common Minimum 
National Action Plan for Power (CMNPP) which envisages, inter alia that: 
No sector shall pay less than 50% of the average cost of supply (cost of 
generation plus transmission and distribution) and that tariffs for agricultural 
sector will not be less than 50 paise/KWH to be brought to 50% of the 
average cost in not more than three years. 
The Government of India have enacted the Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions Act, 1998 with a view to rationalize tariff and providing for 
transparent policies regarding subsidies. The Regulatory Commissions are 
expected to fix tariff so as to progressively reflect the cost of supply, 
encourage efficiency, economy and competition. The Regulatory 
Commissions are also requ ired to ensure that interests of consumers are 
safeguarded and at the same time consumers pay for the use of electricity in a 
reasonable manner based on the average cost of supply. 
The Conference of Chief Ministers/Power Ministers held on 26.2.2000 
recognized that the cross subsidies cannot be sustained if the industrial tariff 
makes industry non-competitive. 
The Chief Ministers/Power Ministers Conference held on 3.3.2001 
resolved inter alia that,

Power reforms 
2302. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of States that have effectively been implementing power 
reforms in the country; 
(b) the transmission and distribution losses in the States which have been 
effectively implementing power reforms in the country; 
(c) whether it is a fact that inspite of reforms T&D losses have noi come 
down; and 
(d) if so, what steps the Ministry is taking to reduce T&D losses? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATIJAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, 
Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi have initiated 
power sector reforms by enacting their own State Electricity Reforms laws 
which provide, inter alia, for unbundling/corporatisation of SEBs, setting up of 
SERCs etc. They have unbundled and corporatised their electricity boards. 
Twelve SERCs of Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, 
Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Rajasthan, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal 
Pradesh and West Bengal have already issued tariff orders. In the MoUs/MoAs 
on reforms with the Ministry of Power, twenty-two States have so far 
committed themselves to having tariffs fixed by SERCs. 
747 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
(b) and (c) A statement indicating the State-wise reported transmission and 
distribution losses in the country is given in Statement. In absence of 100% 
metering the figures of transmission and distribution (T&D) losses are estimates 
and in many States after more accurate estimation, it has been found that 
consumption by this agriculture where supplies are usually not metered was being 
over reported by a considerable margin. This had the effect of disguising 
pilferage in urban areas. Theft of electricity is now estimated to cost over Rs. 
20,000 crore per year. 
(d) A consensus was reached in the Conference of Chief Ministers/ Power 
Ministers held in March, 2001 on the need to depoliticise power sector reforms 
and speed up their implementation and that the real challenge of reforms lies 
in distribution sector. It was resolved in the conference to achieve break even 
in distribution in two years time and achieve positive returns thereafter. It was 
also resolved that State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) would be 
made functional and tariff petition filed and subsidy may be given only to the 
extent of State Government's capacity to pay the subsidies explicitly through budget. 
The Government of India has been signing Memoranda of Understanding (MoU) 
with States reflecting the joint commitment of the Centre and the States to 
undertake reforms in a time bound manner. These require the States to set up 
SERCs, undertake energy audit through full metering, reduce transmission and 
distribution losses and attain commercial viability. In reciprocation to the efforts of 
the States to achieve agreed milestones, the Central Government has committed 
assistance including allocation of additional power from unallocated share from 
Central Generating Stations, funds under specific programmes/schemes etc. The 
MoLls are now being fleshed out into MoAs with clearer and more specific 
milestones as the reform programme in the State is acquiring concrete shape. 
22 States have been covered by this exercise till now. 
The Accelerated Power Development and Reform Programme 
(APDRP) is designed to finance specific projects in identified distribution 
circles for a quick turn around and creation of centres of excellence. Initially, 
63 circles have been taken up for development as centres of excellence on 
the basis of well designed Detailed Project Reports (DPRs). The programme is 
being extended to cover concentrated loads and towns with population of over 1 
lakh where work on repairing DPRs have been initiated. The base line data of 
DPRs is crucial for evaluating the results 
748 
08 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
of the programme which is aimed at improving quality of supply as well as 
controlling theft and improving the financial health of the sector. This 
programme also includes an incentive scheme aiming at actual cash loss 
reduction by SEBs/Utilities. Under this scheme, there is provision for grants 
by the Ministry of Power to SEBs/Utilities for actual loss reduction. 
So far States of Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Uttar 
Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Delhi have unbundled their electricity 
boards. 21 States have notified constitution of State Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions and 12 State Electricity Regulatory Commissions have passed tariff 
orders, which reflect a trend towards tariff rationalization. 
Government of India has recently approved a scheme for securitisation 
of dues owed by the State Electricity Board to CPSUs.The scheme provides 
that 60% of the interest/surcharge on the delayed payments as on 30.9.2001 
would be waived off and the rest of the dues would be securitised through tax-
free bonds issued by the respective State Governments. There would also be 
incentives to the States for timely payment of current dues. DefauK in making 
current payments shall attract, inter alia suspension of funds under APDRR With 
the Securitisation of past dues by the State Government and the creation of the 
discipline of full payment for current supplies, the raising of the requisite 
resources from the market for the ambitious capacity addition programme of 
the CPSUs would become feasible. The State Governments can also use this 
to give their power utilities clean balance sheets to enable them to fully access 
markets for funds to finance their investment programmes.

Yojana (SGSY)" held in June 2001 at Hyderabad, it was resolved to form at least 
one Self-Help Group in each habitation of the Country by Ufa year 2004. There 
are estimated to be about 14 lakh rural habitations in the country. 
The objective of SGSY is to bring the assisted families (Swarozgaris) above 
the Poverty Line by orgnising them into Self-Help Groups (SHGs) through the 
process of social mobilisation, their training and capacity building and 
provision of income generating assets through a mix of Bank credit and

and development of activity clusters by financing selected key activities. The group 
approach helps the rural poor to build their own organisation for socio-

Revision of guidelines for IWDP 
2318. SHRI K. M. KHAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have recently revised 
guidelines for watershed Development under Integrated Wasteland 
Development Programme; 
(b) if so, the salient features of these guidelines; 
(c) the major activities taken up in the projects under the programme during 
last three years, State-wise; 
(d) the number of districts/States in which the programme is being 
implemented; and 
(e) the funding pattern of the programme and total amount sanctioned and 
spent under programme as on 31 st March, 2002? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ANNASAHEB M. K. PAT'IL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Department of Land 
Resources in the Ministry of Rural Development have revised the guidelines for 
Watershed Development in September, 2001. These guidelines are applicable to 
Integrated Wasteland Development Programme  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
771 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
(IWDP), Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP) and Desert Development 
Programme (DDP).The salient features of the Guidelines are to provide greater 
flexibility in implementation, focussed role for Panchayati Raj Institutions, 
twin track approach, exit protocol for Project Implementation Agencies, greater 
community participation in project implementation and post project 
maintenance, provision for availing the credit facility from financial 
institutions, transparency in implementation etc. 
(c)The IWDP is being implemented through projects on watershed basis. 
The watershed treatment plans under these projects are location specific and in 
accordance with the local requirements. The major development activities 
taken up under these projects usually include land development, soil and moisture 
conservation measures (leveling, terracing, bunding, trenching, vegetative barriers, 
gully plugging etc.); water resources development and conservation measures 
(water harvesting structures like check dams, farm ponds, percolation tanks, 
village ponds etc.); afforestation, pasture development and conservation measures 
(fuel wood plantations, fodder trees, ag ro-forestry, silvi-pasture, horticulture 
etc.). 
(d) The projects under IWDP are generally sanctioned in the 
development blocks not covered under DPAP/DDP. At present, the IWDP 
projects are under implementation in 297 districts of 27 States. 
(e)The IWDP is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme. Prior to 1.4.2000, the 
States were provided 100% funding @ Rs. 4000 per hectare. The cost norm 
has been revised w.e.f. 1.4.2000 to Rs.6000 per hectare to be shared by the 
Central and State Governments in the ratio of Rs. 5500 : Rs. 500. During 2001 -
02, the budgetary provision under IWDP at the Central level was Rs. 210 crore and 
the Rs. 169.61 crore was released to the programme States towards 
implementation of on-going watershed projects and sanction of new watershed 
projects.

Fiscal incentives for handloom sector 
2325. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the measures taken to tone up Handloom Sector by the 
Government under the new Textile Policy; 
(b) how far these have benefited the Handloom Sector; 
(c) whether Government propose to give fiscal incentives for 
Handloom Sector; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) and (b)The National Textile Policy, 
2000, provides for the development of training modules for weavers engaged 
in the production of low value items with the objective of upgrading their skills and 
helping them survive the competition consequent on globalization. 
The Office of the Development Commissioner for Handlooms has been 
imparting training to the weavers for capacity building, value addition, product 
diversification etc., under various Schemes such as Development of Exportable 
Products and their Marketing Scheme, Decentralized Training Programme for 
weavers and Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana launched in the year 
2000-01 which, inter alia, provides for skill upgradation of weavers through 
training by Master Weavers. 
The Policy also aims at continuing the implementation of 
comprehensive welfare measures in close cooperation with the State 
Governments for better working environment and the social security of the 
weavers. 
The Office of the Development Commissioner for Handlooms has been 
implementing various schemes for the welfare of weavers, such as Workshed-
cum-Housing Scheme, Health Package Scheme, New Insurance Scheme, Group 
Insurance Scheme and Thrift Fund Scheme. 
The Policy further seeks to provide for effective support system in 
research and development, design inputs, and market linkages. 
In this connection, a project called the National Center for Textile 
Design (NCTD) has been launched to link the weavers with national and 
784 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
international markets; to connect variou s sectors of the textile industry with 
one another; and to provide services to enable the industry to respond better and 
quickly to market demands by providing effective design inputs and colour 
forecast. 
The Policy also provides for the revamping of the Weavers' Service 
Centres in consonance with the contemporary trends and for dovetailing their 
activities suitably with the activities of Centres of Design excellence like 
National Institute of Fashion Technology and National Institute of Design using 
Information Technology for efficiency. 
Out of the total 24 Weavers' Service Centers, 21 Weavers' Service 
Centres have already been linked with the National Center for Textile 
Design. 18 Weavers' Service Centers have been provided with the Computer 
Aided Textile Design System and 20 Centers with computers. The possible areas 
of co-operation between the Weavers' Service Centers and the National Institute 
of Design have been identified. Regular and focused interaction of the 
Weavers Service Centers located at places where centers of National Institute 
of FashionTechnology exist has been established. 
(c) and (d)The following fiscal concessions/exemptions are available to the 
Handloom Sector:— 
(1) The following types of yarn when purchased by a registered 
Handloom Apex Cooperative Society or National/State Handloom 
Development Corporation are exempt from excise duty: 
(a) Yarn of wool; 
(b) Cotton yarn in cross reel hank form; 
(c) yarn of certain blends of polyester/cotton, polyester/viscose; and 
(d) Yarn of counts not exceeding 25 of artificial staple fiber supplied in 
cross reel hanks. 
 
(2) Yarn of upto 2 counts manufactured from cotton wastes on condensor 
card machine in plain reel hanks, is exempt from excise duty. 
(3) The following fabrics produced on handloom and processed by a 
785 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
process house owned by a registered Apex Handloom Co-operative Society 
or a State Handloom Development Corporation are exempt from excise 
duty:— 
(a) Woollen; 
(b) Cotton; and 
(c) Certain blends of polyester/cotton and ployester viscose. 
 
(4) The woollen fabrics produced on handloom and processed by an 
Independent processor approved by Government of India are also 
exempt from excise duty. 
(5) The excise duty on cotton fabrics produced on handlooms and 
processed by an Independent processor approved by Government of India 
is levied at a concessional rate. 
(6) Articles of apparel and made up textile articles made out of handloom fabrics 
are exempt from excise duty. 
Ban by Germany en import of Ejo Coloured clothes from India 
†2326. SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of TEXTILES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the ban imposed 
by Germany on import of such clothes from India wherein Ejo Colour has 
been used; 
(b) if so, whether such clothes contain an excessive quantity of 
carrenojence" in them; and 
(c) if so, the steps taken by Government in this regard and the amount 
of loss the country is likely to suffer as a result of ban on such imports to 
Germany? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHFU BASANGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) to (c) Germany had imposed a 
legislative requirement prohibiting use of specific azo dyes which are harmful 
to human being, in the manufacture of textile products in Germany and imported 
into Germany irrespective of the country in which textile 
†Original notice of the question was reqeived in Hindi. 
 
786 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
items are manufactured. The German requirement for not using specific azo 
dyes releasing any of the 20 harmful amines in the manufacture of textiles 
came into force with effect from 1 st April 1996. As per the method adopted by 
Germany, the presence of each of the amines upto a quantity of 30 ppm is 
permissible. 
The Government has been taking a number of measures to assist the 
textile trade industry and exporters in India to meet the challenges posed by the 
ecological requirements imposed by Germany. Some of the initiatives are as 
under: 
(i) The Textile Committee, Textiles Research Association,. Export 
Promotion Councils and other organizations organised a number of 
seminars and workshop at all the textile centres for creating 
awareness about the German ban and for providing guidance for the 
manufacture of eco-friendly textiles. 
(ii) Government have prohibited the handling 112 dyes which are capable 
of releasing any of the harmful amines under usage through 
reductive cleavage process. 
(iii) The Government of India has further set up 23 laboratories, in different 
parts of the country, with sophisticated instruments capable of 
testing textiles to assess their conformance as per the requirements 
of Germany. 
As a result of the various measures taken, the usage of harmful dyes and 
chemicals in manufacturing of textiles and apparels, particularly those meant for 
exports has come down significantly since 1996. India's textile and clothing 
industry is in a position to effectively meet the situation arising out of German ban 
and there has been no downfall in textile exports to Germany on account of 
inability of our industry to meet these eco-specification.

Textile Exports to US 
2329. SHRIRAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister 
of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India's export of textiles to the US in dollar terms has 
declined during 2001 ; 
(b) whether as compared to India's exports to the US and exports of China, 
Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh have increased in this period; 
(c) the reasons for fall in India's exports and increase in neighbouring 
countries' exports; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to boost exports of textiles to the US? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) India's textile exports to US during the 
year 2001 -02 amounted to US$ 2556.5 million as against the exports of US$ 
3139.6 million during the year 2000-01, recording a negative growth of 18.6%. 
792 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The major immediate reasons for slow/negative growth 
of our textile exports in recent months are the reduced global demand triggered 
by the slowdown in the economies of some of our major trading partners like US, 
September 11 events, Afghanistan war, increasing polarization of world trade, 
formation of preferential trading blocks and stiff competition from low cost 
suppliers like Bangladesh, China, etc. particularly in the price sensitive range 
where bulk of our textile exports are concentrated. 
(d) Government have been taking several steps from time to time to boost 
textile exports to various countries including US. Some of the important 
initiatives are:— 
(i) The Government has de-reserved the woven segment of readymade 
garment from the SSI sector. 
(ii) TheTechnology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1.4.1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(iii) Weaving, processing and garment machinery, which are covered under 
TUFS, have been extended the facility of accelerated depreciation at 
the rate of 50%. Cost of machinery has also been reduced through Fiscal

Labour abuse 
*361. SHRIJIBON ROY: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
"India rapped on labour abuse" published in the Times of India' dated the 20th 
June, 2002; and 
(b) if so, Government's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SAHIB SINGH VERMA): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. The main  points raised in the news-item which relate to a 
report by the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) are 
(i) abuse of Core Labour Standards, (ii) widespread child labour, (iii) 
employment of child labour in export related sectors, (iv) absence of freedom 
to protest resulting in death of ,17 workers and their family members inTamil 
Nadu for demanding increase in poverty wages, and (v) ICFTU's request to 
WTO to work intensively with the Government of India. However, no such 
report has been received by the Government. 
The position with reference to the above issues is as under: 
India supported the adoption of the ILO Declaration on 
* The sitting of the Rajya Sabha on Thursday, the 8th August, 2002 was

the lists for that day were laid on the Table of the House on Monday, the 12th

800 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work, 1998. Consequently, the 
principles enshrined in the Core Labour Standards of the ILO are being 
implemented for the benefit of workers through national laws and 
development programmes. The allegation that all core labour standards are 
being abused is not accepted, such instances as come to the notice of the 
concerned Governments are dealt with appropriately. 
As regards ICFTU's suggestion that WTO should work intensively with 
the Government of India in relation to child labour, India's stand has been that 
the ILO is the only appropriate forum tor-addressing the issues relating to the 
international labour standards. This is also in consonance with the declaration 
of the WTO Ministerial Conference held in 1996 in Singapore and has been 
reiterated in subsequent Ministerial Conferences as well. India has 
consistently rejected any attempts at a linkage between trade and labour 
standards, as such a linkage is seen as a protectionist device meant to hinder 
the comparative advantage of low wage developing economies. 
As far as widespread child labour is concerned, the number of children in India 
who are working as child labour is 11.28 million as per 1991 census.The 
National Policy on Child Labour in India provides for abolition of child labour 
through a sequential process beginning with the worst forms and thereafter 
moving to hazardous and less hazardous forms of child labour. The Policy 
envisages a multi-pronged strategy for addressing the problem. Under the area 
based component of the strategy a scheme of National Child Labour Projects 
(NCLPs) was formulated and is currently being implemented in 100 districts 
spread over 13 child labour endemic States in India. The Government had 
allocated around Rs. 250 crore for the last Five Year Plan for utilisation in 
these projects. 
As far as the alleged excesses by the Police against workers in Tamil 
Nadu is concerned, the Government of Tamil Nadu has intimated that there has 
been no incident where workers were killed because they demanded increase 
in wages.

Statement 
Reaction of foreign countries over Gujarat carnage 
Some countries of the world officially expressed their reactions over 
Godhara and the communal riots in Gujarat. The reactions of these countries 
are as follows: 
Pakistan 
On March 2,2002, President General Pervez Musharraf, expressed dismay 
and sorrow over large-scale communal violence in India and said that violence 
against the Muslim community had caused deep distress and concern among 
the people of Pakistan. 
In a statement, President Musharraf said that the incident could not provide 
license for the reprehensible brutalities and violence against the Muslim 
community that had caused hundreds of deaths, destruction of property and 
desecration of Muslim religious places.  He said the measures taken by the 
Government of India for the protection of its Muslim minority, which is the target 
of Hindu extremism and terror, needed to be strengthened. He said that the 
carnage must be brought to an end and all those responsible for the violence be 
arrested and punished. 
President Musharraf said the violence and mayhem in India had again 
highlighted the damages posed by politics of communalism and the forces of 
extremism & terrorism.The International community cannot afford to be 
complacent or take a biased view in responding to and combating this evil in 
whichever form it manifested and wherever it existed, he added. 
According to APP report (1.3.02) in response to a question about the 
communal violence in Gujarat, the Pakistani Foreign Office spokesman stated that 
while law and order inside India was an internal matter of that country, the 
government of Pakistan deeply regretted the loss and property in the recent 
incidents. He also said the Government of Pakistan sympathised with all those 
who suffered as a result of the violence and offered its condolences to the 
breaved families. 
811 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
When his attention was drawn to the allegation by the Indian Defence 
Minister, as reported in a section of the Press, that Pakistan's ISI was behind 
these disturbances, the spokesman termed its as ridiculous and irresponsible. 
China 
Though no official comments/statement were made/issued by the 
Government of China, the Spokesman of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs 
on our Prime Minister's alleged remarks about Muslims said at a press 
conference on 16th April, 2002 that they "have not read the relevant speech. 
However, it is our hope that India could maintain social stability as well as 
unity and harmony among its ethnic groups." 
Bangladesh 
The Government of Bangladesh did not officially express any reaction over 
the Godhara incident and communal riots. However, through a Note Verbale of 
May 12,2002 to our High Commission in Dhaka, it referred to the incident in 
Godhara and Informed the Government of India about Bengali speaking families 
from India trying to flee and allegedly attempting crossover into Bangladesh 
as a result of the violence due to the riots in Gujarat. It was also alleged in the 
note verbale that BSF was actively involved in trying to push these families 
into Bangladesh. In response to the note verbale, our High Commission 
conveyed to the Government of Bangladesh that in the context of Government of 
India's concern regarding large scale illegal migration from Bangladesh, there 
was no question of BSF of India trying to push them into their home country, 
since these families had come to India from Bangladesh. Details were also 
requested from Government of Bangladesh on any Indian national who may 
have returned to Bangladesh from India. Govt, of Bangladesh was also informed 
that the situation in Gujarat was being brought under control and suitable action 
against those found to be indulging in violence was being taken by the 
Government of India. 
Iran 
The Spokesperson of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic 
Republic of Iran made an official statement on Gujarat events on March 2,2002. 
He strongly deplored wide-scale unrest and violence of the past few days and 
said that Iran was hopeful that Indian government would 
812 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
overcome the problem with full capability by exercising tolerance. He said that it 
was expected that leaders of the Muslims and Hindu communities will 
demonstrate self-restraint and concentrate their efforts on building mutual 
understanding and dialogue, that will lead to prosperity. 
During a meeting atTehran with President Seyed Mohammad Khatami of Iran 
on March 31, 2002, Minister of State for External Affairs, Shri Omar 
Abdullah, who was visiting Iran as Special Envoy of the Prime Minister, stressed 
upon the Indian government's commitment to secularism. He said that we moved 
fast to contain the spread of violence to other states and will ensure that there 
is no repeat of such violence in the affected areas. 
New Zealand 
Hon'ble Phil Goff, Minister of Foreign Affairs andTrade of New Zealand in a 
letter dated 2nd April, 2002 addressed to our High Commissioner in Wellington 
expressed "deep concern about the communal unrest in Gujarat". He added 
that media reports of the conflict have been quite shocking and especially 
disturbing for the New Zealand Indian Community. However, he further stated that 
it was encouraging to note that communal conflict appeared to have subsided for 
the last week or so. In response, our High Commissioner through a letter 
addressed to Hon"ble Pljil Goff provided detailed information on the subject 
especially various preventive and confidence building measures including peaceful 
conduct of secondary school examination; elections to the village Panchayats, 
appointments of Justice S.D. Dave to hold judicial enquiry into incidednt of 
attack on journalists; visit by Prime Minister to Gujarat, etc. 
Europe 
U.K. 
Statements on the communal violence in Gujarat were made by Prime 
MinisterTony Blair, Foreign Secretary Straw and other British officials. In these 
statements, the British Government expressed its concern over local casualities 
and over the safety of British citizens in the State. It also appreciated the efforts 
of Government of India to restore calm. 
Germany 
German Foreign Minister made the following statement on March 1, 
813 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
2002:—"The German Government condemns the violent riots in Gujarat. It is 
shocked and concerned about the terrible images of dead and the injured as 
well as burning houses, all the more so because his confrontation is taking place 
between supporters of two major world religions.The German Government urges 
the leaders of the groups involved to end the confrontation.The prudent stand 
taken by the Indian Government, which is pressing for a peaceful solution to the 
conflict based on the rule of law, deserves our recognition." 
France 
There was no official statement or comment by the French Government. 
However, in response to a question asking whether the riots in India which left at 
least 200 dead were linked to the crisis in Central Asia, the official 
Spokesperson of the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs replied, "We 
profoundly deplore such violence but I have no other comments." 
European Union 
The EL) General Affairs Council consisting of EU Foreign Ministers 
adopted a Declaration on 15th April 2002 in which it also expressed its

Even though events in Gujarat are strictly an internal matter of the

• The KVIC is unable to meet its employment generation of 20 lakh 
additional jobs in the 8th Plan. 
• It created 8.01 lakh additional employment in Khadi (0.5) and VI 
(7.42) both part-time and full time. The full time employment in 1996-
97 have earned Rs. 4835 in Khadi Sector and Rs. 4323 in V.I. sector. 
• While employment growth in Khadi sector was negligible in 8th Plan, 
in V.I. sector it grew @ 4.14% per annum. 
• About 95% of additional employment generated during 8th Plan was 
in the V.I. sector. 
• In Khadi sector, the physical out-put of cloth remain more or less 
constant and so did the labour productivity. The additional budgetary 
resources (grant and rebate) allocated to the Khadi sector seem to be 
getting absorbed year after without any corresponding increase in 
employment, out-put in sales realization.

• A comprehensive evaluation of KVI training institutions be conducted 
and necessary steps be taken to revamp and reorient the training 
methods so that training helps contribute to labour productivity and 
development of khadi and village industries.

belonging to the families below the poverty line, about 71 % have 
actually cross the poverty line with the help of additional income from 
KVIC programme. The performance of the VI sector far outways that of 
the Khadi sector.

gainful employment opportunities for the rural poor arresting migration 
of rural unskilled workers to urban areas and promoting the strategy of 
sustainable development. Potential cannot be realized without 
changing the design and implementation of the programme.

decision making level is to examine the need for having two 
implementing agencies viz. Khadi Commission and Village 
Industries Commission. The Khadi Commission in the Ministry of 
Textiles and the V.I. Commission under the Ministry of SSI&ARI.

Handloom sector eliminated by yam requirement from the Khadi 
sector.

private sector while some processed goods be produced by the KVIC

monitor flow of inputs and outputs and the Commission should be made 
accountable to inputs and output relationship.

Commission. In the new scenario, no rebate on sale is

(d) whether the company propose to offer any kind of incentives to the 
customers to woo them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 
(SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) to (c) Sir, as a result of tenders 
invited during the year 2001 for grant of licences for Cellular Mobile 
Telephone Service (CMTS); M/s Bharti Cellular Limited were granted 
licences for CMTS operation in 1800 MHz Band for 8 new Service Areas in 
September, 2001. As per the information furnished by M/s Bharti Cellular Limited, 
it has started CMTS in 7 out of these 8 new Service Areas namely Mumbai, 
Gujarat, Haryana, Kerala, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, UP-West 
and is likely to launch service in due course in the only remaining Gujarat 
Telecom Circle Servtce Area. 
As per the terms and conditions of the CMTS Licence, an operator is 
required to cover 10% of District Headquarters within one year and 50% of 
District Headquarters within three years. The Licensee is also permitted to 
cover any other town in a district in lieu of the District Headquarter. The 
choice of District Headquarters / towns to be covered and further expansion 
beyond 50% District Headquarters/towns shall He with, the Licensee depending 
on their business decision. 
Government does not exercise control with regard to the choice of cities / 
areas to be covered with the service by a private company and also does not 
keep record of the investment made by a private company. 
(5) telecom Regulatory Authorfty of India (TRAI) is responsible for

Provision of village telephones by BSNL and DoT 
2367. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) what has been the precentageof village telephones provided by the 
public sector BSNL and DoT during the last three years and what is the 
percentage of telephones installed as against the number of DELs installed 
from 1998 to 2001; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Attorney General of India has opined before 
migration to the National Telecom Policy, 1999, that two sets of licensing 
regimes were legally not tenable to the growth of telecom; and 
(c) whether Government have accepted this recommendation or 
continuing with two sets of licenses in the telecom sector? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORM4TCN TECHNOLOGY (SHRIMATI 
SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) BSNL and erstwhile DoT were providing 
telephones in urban areas as well as rural areas in the villages during last three 
years. Total DELs installed is 14.91 million and 17.76 per cent of this DELs are 
Village Telephones (Rural Area Telephones). Total Village PublicTelephones 
(VPT) provided during last three year is 1,29,057 and this is 44.52% of the target 
fixed for VPTs during last three years. 
(b) and (c) Opinion of the Attorney General was sought by the 
Government in the context of Government's intention expressed in New 
Telecom Policy-1999 (NTP-99) to "satisfactorily resolve the problems being faced 
by the existing operators in a manner which is consistent with the contractual 
obligations and is legally tenable" (Para 3.11 of NTP-99).The existing operators 
were facing problems due to high licence fees committed in the bids submitted by 
them for obtaining the licences. In his opinion the Attorney General had, inter-
alia, expressed that "continuance of existing 
861 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
licensees under the 1994 Telecom Policy regime and its enforcement currently 
with NTP-99 will create problems, which will not be beneficial." It was further 
opined that migration of licensees to NTP-99 is warranted and that such 
migration should not be retrospective but from a prospective date to be decided 
by the Government. It should be ensured that defaulting licensees are not totally 
absolved of the contractual obligations voluntarily undertaken by them under the 
Licence Agreements and migration should be subject to certain conditions with 
regard to payment of arrears of licence fees. 
The Government decided migration policy after considering the 
opinion of the Attorney General, and shifted the existing operators from fixed 
licence fee regime to revenue sharing regime of the New Telecom Policy-1999; 
however, their all other contractual obligations, inter-alia, rollout of services, 
provision of Village Public Telephones etc. remain unchanged.

Marketing of fake consumer goods 
2385. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a number of fake consumer goods are being 
marketed in the country on a large scale; 
(b) if so, the stringent measures taken to control the menace; and 
(c) whether Government would contemplate any long term strategy to 
curb the practice? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTH E MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRIV. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) to (c)TheTrade & Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 which deals 
with the registration and licensing of trade marks seeks to protect the 
intellectual poverty inherent in a trade mark and includes provisions for 
safeguarding the rights of the registered trade mark owner through various 
provisions which need to be agitated in the civil/criminal court. However, the 
onus of seeking to protect his right lies entirely upon the registered holder of 
trade mark. Further, standards of quality of various consumer goods are notified 
by different agencies under different laws. For instance, Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare (Department of Health) notify standards of quality of various 
articles of food under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, 
compliance to which is mandatory.Similarly, the Bureau of Indian Standards 
(BIS) is notifying quality standards for various items including consumer 
goods. Conformance to such standards is voluntary unless made mandatory 
under any law. Conformance to standards notified by BIS has been made 
mandatory in respect of some products. Such products are required to carry 
the BIS Standards Mark (ISI) which can be used by manufacturers licensed to 
do so by the BIS. Cases of spurious ISI mark which come to the notice of BIS 
are investigated and prosecution launched in suitable cases. During the three 
years 1999-2000 to 2001 -2002, BIS launched prosecution in 53 cases for 
alleged misuse of the BIS standards mark.

Services provided by BIS 
2392. SHRILAJPAT RAI: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the recent steps taken by Government to increase the services 
provided by BIS in various parts of the country, specifically to Northern 
India; 
(b) the reasons for the shortage of technical manpower; 
(c) what are the differences between the different certifications such as 
product certification, quality mangement certification etc.; and 
(d) the products that have been given the BIS mark by the State level 
Committee in Punjab? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD) (a)To cater to the needs of industries and consumers, Bureau of 
Indian Standards (BIS) has established its Branch Offices in various parts of 
the country including five Offices in Northern India at Chandigarh, Kanpur, 
Lucknow, Faridabad and Nalagarh.The Branch office at Nalagrah has been 
opened recently. To facilitate convenient accessibility to the services provided 
by BIS, it has also launched its own website at http:// www.bis.org.in. which 
contains complete information about the organization and the services offered by 
it. 
(b) Vacancies in BIS are filled up as per guidelines issued by the 
Central Government from time to time. 
(c)The details are given in the enclosed Statement (See below) 
(d)The State level Committees are not empowered to grant licenses for use 
of BIS Mark. 
Statement 
Details of the various certification schemes of Bureau of Indian 
Standards 
i) Product Certification Scheme  - Under this scheme licences are 
granted to manufacturers for using the BIS Standard mark (Popularly 
known as ISI mark) on their products after the manufacturers 
have been found suitable through pre-licence 
891 

 
RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
inspection, testing of samples and evaluation of technical 
competence. After grant of certification of quality of the products 
certified is checked through regular surveillance on the 
manufactures set-up and testing of samples taken from the factory 
as well as from the market.The products are regularly tested in the 
Bureau's own laboratory as well as laboratories recognized for this 
purpose. 
ii) Quality Systems Certification Scheme - Under this scheme product 
manufacturing firms as well as service providers are granted 
licences for using the Quality Systems Certification Mark of the 
Bureau after their quality management systems have been found to 
be conforming to ISO 9001 or ISO 9002 International Standards. 
After grant of licence surveillance visits are carried out regularly to 
ensure that the licensed organizations are maintaining the norms required 
underthese standards. Under this scheme, licences have also been 
granted for certification of food safety to those manufacturers who 
have installed check points in the food chain according to Indian 
Standard IS 15000: 1998 Hazard Analysis & Critical Control Points. 
iii) Environment Systems Certification - Under this scheme 
organizations who maintain environment protection norms 
according to ISO 14000 series of International Standards are 
granted licences. 
iv)  Hallmarking of Gold Jewell ery - Under this scehem the BIS 
certifies the jewellers for purity of Gold and also gives 
recognition to Assaying and Hallmarking Centres that conduct the 
testing for purity of gold. 
v) Certification of Foreign Manufacturers and Indian Importer's 
Scheme - Under this scheme the quality of goods being imported 
into India can be certified either by granting licences to 
manufacturers situated in a foreign country or to importer situated 
in India.This scheme operates in a manner similar to BIS Product 
Certification Scheme. 
C AGs criticism of foodgrain prices 
2393. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Comptroller and Auditor General of India has criticized the 
Centre's policy on prices of foodgrains; 
892 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action taken to set right the shortcomings pointed out by the CAG? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI U. V. KRISHNAM* 
RAJU): (a) to (c)The C&AG in its Report 2000-01 made certain observations on 
prices of foodgrains.The main observations are the following: 
(i) The price movements show a policy tilt towards producers vis a 'vis 
purchasers; 
(ii) The inevitable increase in subsidies in the short run and in Central Issue 
Prices thereafter reduced the margins between the PDS prices and the 
market prices which led to the decline in offtake of foograins in some 
years; 
(iii) Despite foodgrains availability in the public domain, the aggregate 
release of foodgrains remained static between 1992-99; 
(iv) The procurement price for wheat was higher, and it is certainly not to 
the advantage of the consumer; 
(v) The leakages and inefficiencies at the level of Procurement and 
Release Agencies and also some other costs added at State level 
increase the prices for consumers as a result of which 60 to 70 per cent 
ration card holders did not/do not purchase rice or wheat from the 
fair price shops. 
The Central Issue Prices (CIP) of wheat and rice are fixed by the 
Government mainly to help the poorest & the disadvantaged segments of our 
population. As such, under the TPDS, wheat and rice are issued to BPL 
families at subsidized rates.The CIPs fixed for APL families also contain an 
element of subsidy. Therefore, CIPs are not at par with the open market 
prices which depend on free play of demand and supply. However, the 
economic cost of wheat and rice are kept in mind while fixing the CIPs. 
The Government has taken various measures to increase the offtake as per 
the enclosed Statements.

Bhutan 
The presence of ULFA militants on Bhutanese territory has been a subject 
of discussion with the Government of Bhutan. Both sides share concern on the 
issue.The Government of Bhutan has reiterated that they 
920 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
would not allow their territory to be misused against the interests ot India. 
The King of Bhutan, in his National Day address on December 17, 2001, 
called the presence of armed militants from Assam on Bhutanese soil as the

National Assembly of Bhutan adopted a series of Resolutions in 1999,2000 and

Assembly held in July, 2002, reiterated the urgency to evict the militants from

Committee on 22.7.98 under the Chairmanship of Shri S.R. Sathyam to review 
the services provided in the ESI Hospitals/Dispensaries. The Committee 
submitted its report on 14.1.1999. 
The short term recommendations of the Sathyam Committee such as

drugs, purchase of medicines in strip packs, provision of medicines for supply by 
the hospitals or specialist clinics for a minimum period, streamlining the 
purchase procedure with adequate delegation of powers, have been accepted. 
The long term recommendations like parity in all respects with 
medical officers of ESI Scheme and their counterparts in the general health 
services, contractual arrangements for running ambulance services, cleaning, 
security, laundry, kitchen and maintenance of equipments etc. have been 
approved. 
Recommendation such as grant of exemption in the event of both the

Rise in Unemployment 
2436. SHRI CHO. S. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that unemployment is gradually on the rise all over 
the country; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) what steps are being taken to control unemployment in the country; 
(d) the number of unemployed in the country as on the 31 st March, 2002; 
and 
(e) what is the impact of Government's disinvestments policy 
vis-a-vis unemployment problem in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) and (b) Estimates of employment and 
unemployment are obtained through Labour Force Surveys conducted by 
National Sample Survey Organisation from time to time. As per these surveys, 
estimated number of unemployed persons in the country based on Usual 
Principal and Subsidiary Status (UPSS) approach has marginally gone up from 
about 7.5 million in 1993-94 to 9.0 million in 1999-2000. Lack of growth of 
the economy at the desired rate and the mismatch in the demand and supply of 
manpower in the labour market are some of the major reasons for increase in 
unemployment. 
(c) The Tenth Plan will focus on providing gainful high quality 
employment to the additions to the labour force and it will be one of the 
monitorable objectives for the 10th Plan and beyond.The growth strategy of the 
10th Plan would lay emphasis on the rapid growth of those sectors which are 
likely to create high quality employment opportunities and deal with the policy 
constraints which discourage growth of employment. Particular attention would 
be paid to the policy environment influencing a wide range of economic 
activities which have a large employment potential. 
(d) Estimated number of unemployed persons as on January, 2000 based 
on Usual Principal and Subsidiary Status (UPSS) approach was of the order of 9 
million. 
934

(e) So far, there has been no retrenchment in any of the public sector 
enterprises which have been privatized through the process of disinvestment. 
Strategic disinvestments of public sector undertakings with transfer of 
management control to strategic partners do not normally affect the status of 
employment since the employees of the public sector undertakings continue to 
remain in employment even after disinvestments of the PSUs, subject to the 
agreements entered into between the Government and the strategic partners.

TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (MAJOR GENERAL (RETD.) B.C.

966 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(i)  The registration number of vehicles shall be hot stamped and

chromium based sticker shall be affixed on the left hand top side of the 
wind shield of four- wheelers. The engine number, chasis number,

colour scheme on the existing registration plates i.e. letters and figures in 
black colour on yellow background in case of transport vehicles and in black 
colour on white background in case of other vehicles had been mandated on 
or before 1 st February, 2002 in respect of transport vehicles and on or before

Child malnutrition 
*384. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 47 per cent of child population suffers from 
severe malnutrition in India, as reported by UNICEF; 
(b) whether Government have any plan to address this problem; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government have ever conducted any specific studies or 
asked any social or academic units to do so; 
(e) if so, what are the results of these studies; and 
(f) the remedial measures Government propose, to rectify this sad state of 
affairs? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (f)The World Summit for Children, 1990 had 
laid down the goal of reduction in moderate and severe malnutrition among under-
five children, between 1990 and 2000 by half. For India the underweight 
prevalence declined by 6.4% as compared to the decline of 4% for developing 
countries. 
According to UNICEF's publication titled "Progress since the World 
Summit for Children—a statistical review," 47% of under five children are 
underweight in India. 
According to studies, there is a declining trend in prevalence of 
underweight in children under five years as given in Statement {see below). 
However, the problem of malnutrition is multi-dimensional and inter-
generational in nature, which needs to be tackled through holistic and 
coordinated interventions in areas of nutrition, food security, sanitation and 
safe drinking water, health & family welfare, and poverty alleviation. 
Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme, which aims at 
holistic development of children in the age group of 0-6 years and pregnant 
and lactating mothers, is the largest and most comprehensive intervention

school education, immunization, health check-up, referral services and 
nutrition & health education. Evaluation of ICDS has shown that its impact has 
been significant in reducing IMR and levels of malnutrition.

Climate Change and Agricultural Production 
2502.  SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the global warming has an impact on Indian agriculture which 
would result in up to 30 per cent drop in crop production by 2050; 
(b) if so, whether the Government are considering to adopt strategies and 
resource conserving technologies, for sustainable farm development and 
improved productivity through low cost mechanism; 
(c) whether this would have an impact on rice and wheat yields; 
(d) if so, whether this was discussed in the South Asia Expert 
Workshop on Adaptation to Climate Change for Agricultural Productivity 
held in May, 2002; and 
1013 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
(e) if so, what were the main points discussed in the workshop? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRIHUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (c)There is considerable 
uncertainty in the magnitude of global warming and its impact on agricultural 
production by the year 2050.The Inter-governmental Panel on Climate 
Change (IPCC), jointly establsihed in 1988 by the World Meteorological 
Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme 
(UNEP), in itsThird Assessment Report finanlized in 2001 has projected that 
global average surface temperature may increase by 1.4° C to 5.8° C over the 
period 1990-2100. The IPCC report specifically considers agriculture as highly 
vulnerable to impacts of climate change in the South Asian Region. Crop 
production and aquaculture would be threatend by thermal and water stresses, 
sea-level rise, increased flooding, and strong winds associated with intense 
tropical cyclones. The specific effect of global warming on Indian 
Agriculture, including rice and wheat would depend upon the actual change in 
temperature and other climatic features together with adaptation and mitigation 
strategies. 
(b) Ministry of Agriculture has been adopting various resource 
conservation programmes and schemes to promote efficient utilization of water, 
land, nutrients and pesticides etc. for sustainable farm development in the country. 
Some major programmes and schemes are as under: 
1. National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas 
(NWDPRA). 
2. Soil conservation for Enhancing Productivity of Degraded lands in the 
catchments of River Valley Projects and Flood Prone Rivers. 
3. Reclamation of alkali soils. 
4. Watershed Development Project in Shifting Cultivation Areas 
(WDSCA). 
5. National Project on Development and Use of Bio-fertilisers. 
6. Promotion of Integrated Pest Management. 
7. National Project on organic farming. 
8. Promotion of zero tillage. 
9. Promotion of drip and sprinkler irrigation under the scheme 
Development of Horticulture through Plasti-culture Intervention. 
1014 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(d) and (e)Yes sir. Main goal of the South Asia Expert Workshop on 
Adaptation to Climate Change for Agricultural Productivity held in May 2002 
had two objectives; (i) to increase awareness in the the region of the impact of 
climate change on agriculture and about the existence of potential solutions, (ii) to 
make recommendations to the Eighth Conference of Parties (COP8) of the UN 
Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) being hosted in New 
Delhi in October 2002. The workshop discussed vulnerability, adaptation and 
mitigation issues of Agriculture in the South Asian Region. Some key 
recommendations arrived at in the Workshop are as follows: 
1. Sustainable development policies and programmes in areas such as 
watershed development, promotion of resource conserving technologies, 
natural resource management and development of plant varieties should be 
taken as no regret measures and need to be supported and strengthened. 
2. Adaptation science and policies should be holistic i.e., farming systems 
based rather than single commodity or single discipline. 
3. There is a need for adopting an action-based framework/guidelines by 
mainstreaming adaptation into national and regional planning policies. 
The major components of such a framework would be: 
 
• A cafeteria of programmes and projects, which could be adopted by 
national governments. 
• Provide additional support to on-going governmental programmes, which 
have an adaptation element to combat climate change. 
• Provide incentive structure for those promoting adaptation. Role of 
farmers mitigating greenhouse gases need to be positively recognized 
within the Clean Development Mechanism of the Kyoto Protocol. 
• Promote capacity building programmes. 
• Provide for networking of international, regional and national 
institutions for experience sharing. 
• Documentation of best practices and its dissemination to the 
farmers. 
• Monitoring and evaluation of adaptation process. 
1015 

RAJYA  SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
4. There is need of strengthening public research on adaptation for both 
international as well as national research systems. 
5. International funding support shall be required for the operationali-zation 
of necessary adaptation and mitigation measures.

Andaman & Nicobar Islands which, inter alia, include the following:

parks, sanctuaries and tribal reserves. For other areas, revised 
working plans will be submitted to the Court.

Institute for Disaster Management in Bhopal 
†2566. SHRISURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any proposal/recommendations to establishing a 
Biological Institution for the long term study and research on ill effects of 
Bhopal Gas tragedy and to set up a national level institution for Disaster 
Management in Bhopal has been received by Government; 
(b) if so, by when Government are going to take decision in this regard; 
and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor by Government despite the fact that 
Bhopal suffered the most frightening Industrial accident Bhopal Gas 
tragedy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) to (c) The proposal for 
establishing a Biological Institute has been received with the request that it could 
be funded from the unspent money lying with Reserve Bank of India out of the 
compensation money given by the Union Carbide Company. According to Supreme 
Court directions, the money received from the Union Carbide is earmarked for 
paying compensation to the Bhopal Gas victims. All the compensation claims 
have not yet been decided. On the proposal of setting up a National level 
institution on Disaster Management, the State Government has been advised to 
take up the matter with the concerned Ministry in the Central Government.

Railway Policy 
2614. SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH'LIBRA': 
DR. ABRAR AHMED: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are seriously considering to lay down a 
National Railway Policy, in the near future; if so, the details thereof; and 
1112 

[12 August, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) the progress made, so far. in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) and (b) IX Five Year Plan 
document spells out Railways' policy. It envisages the need for strengthening 
capacity of the Indian Railway system as the prime carrier of long distance 
bullk freight and passenger traffic. For achieving this objective, Railways 
will concentrate on multiplexing and electrification of dense corridors, 
improvement in reliability of operations, containeration of smalls and 
optimisation of total system operations. 
Further Policy framework and strategies conceived in the Plan 
document are summed as under: 
(i) Augment capacity and improve the productivity, which would be 
the basis for decelerating the decline of the share of Railways and 
then reversing the present trend. 
(ii) A flexible freight policy and better Operational and Commercial 
Management, aggressive revenue generation, rigorous cost 
control. 
(iii) Rationalization of Freight and Fares—Keeping subsidies at 
minimum—sufficient flexibility in freight rates to deal with 
market fluctuations as well as in the Fares to deal with the demand 
during peak season. 
(iv) Reprioritise all project portfo lios and early comp letion of ongoing 
works by scrapping unviable projects. 
(v) Improvement in the productivity of the Assets and reducing the 
instance of asset failures—rigrous cost control and proper 
inventory management to improve the productivity of assets. 
(vi) Better Safety standards by means of modern equipments. 
(vii) The role of Private sector should be encouraged in investments in 
Railway infrastructure, Terminal operations and marketing of 
special freight trains. 
The above policy framework continue to be the focus of Railway 
Planning. Railway Policy during the Xth Plan period is in the process of 
approvals.

Bio-Technology in agriculture sector 
2630. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE ANDTECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of achievements in application of Bio-Technology in 
Agriculture sector, especially in Rice, Horticulture and Sericulture; 
(b) whether the Ministry has conducted any training programme in the 
country at the appropriate level, for the application of Bio-Technology in 
Agriculture; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) Agricultural bio-
technology has been accorded high priority since the inception of Department 
of Biotechnology. A number of programmes in this area since 1989, as R&D 
projects, the establishment of seven Centres for Plant Molecular Biology 
(CPMB) and large scale field demonstrations have been taken up. A number of 
multi-institutional projects on development of transgenics, quality 
improvement in wheat and rice have been initiated. Transformation system in 
important cultivars of rice has been developed successfully. Also, controlled 
open field trials of Bt-transgenic indica cultivar, IR-64 and Pusa Basmati-1 
for resistance to yellow stem borer are likely to be conducted soon. Work on 
the other aspects like marker assisted selection for biotic and abiotic stress 
tolerance, bacterial leaf blight, DNA fingerprinting, hybrid rice production and 
development of Indian golden rice varieties has given important leads. In June 
2000, India joined 
1127 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2002] 
International Rice Genome Sequencing Programme (IRGSP), a consortium 
comprising of ten countries. Sequence data of 8.8 Mb in the International Gene 
Bank against our commitment of 2.0 Mb has already been submitted. Complete 
regeneration/micropropagation protocols for important priority crops like 
Banana, Apple, Citrus, Litchi, Potato, Sugarcane etc. have been developed. The 
technology packages are available for Banana, Potato microtubers and minortubers 
and Sugarance. Demonstrations have been conducted in the farmers field for 
transfer of technology at grass root level. In the area of sericulture, an integrated 
pest management package (IPM) comprising uzicide and release of parasitoid 
(Nesoynx thymus) developed to control uzifly a serious pest of silkworm at 
farmers level has been successful. For quality improvement a process has been 
developed for degumming of silk with fungal proteases as valuable alternative. 
Under silkworm genome programme, more than 375 DNA markers have been 
developed and used for fingerprinting of solkworm. 
(b) and (c) Regular training programmes/courses are being conducted in the 
area of agricultural biotechnology. All the CPMB's had an in-built component 
of training. In the area of biofertilizers/biopesticides more than 5000 training 
courses were organized during the last 5 years. At least six such courses in the 
area of tissue culture and biotechnology were conducted both by DBT and 
ICAR.These have to a great extent addressed the training requirements of the 
farming community.

2638.  SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some inputs into steel industry like coal, 
power, railway, freight, prices of diesel and petrol and wages of workers, are 
Administratively controlled by Government departments, with the result that 
steel prices are currently market oriented and go up or down, depend ng upon 
market forces;

anomaly, so that Indian steel companies can compete with global companies; 
and

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI 
BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) The cost of raw materials, power, freight 
and fuel are determined by the pricing policies of the concerned Departments/ 
agencies. These pricing policies are themselves being influenced, in an 
increasing measures, by the market forces. The wage structure in steel 
industry is determined by the wage review mechanism of the public sector/ 
private sector steel units. Besides these factors, cost of production, and 
consequently the pricing of steel products, are also determined by factors 
such as scale of production, technology adopted, locational advantages, cost 
of capital etc. Thus prices of various steel items are decided, in the ultimate 
analysis, by the interplay of various market forces. 
(b) and (c)There is no anomaly in regard to pricing of steel products. 
After decontrol of steel items in 1991 -92 as part of the process of economic
